works: Around the World in Eighty Days
infoBite: Fogg: Around the World in Eighty Days (1872); Don Quixote (1605, 1615); Candide (1759), where Pangloss says all is for the best; Dogberry and Verges are the bumbling watchmen in Much Ado About Nothing.

question: Which one of the following is a famous detective character created by Edgar Allan Poe?
works: The Murders in the Rue Morgue
infoBite: C. Auguste Dupin first appears in “The Murders in the Rue Morgue” (1841), often called the first modern detective story. Maigret is Simenon's, Miss Marple Christie's, Arsène Lupin Leblanc's.

question: “The horror! The horror!” - these are the last words of ______ .
infoBite: Kurtz's dying words, reported by Marlow. Heart of Darkness was serialised in Blackwood's (1899); Achebe attacked it in “An Image of Africa” (1975). Also asked in GATE 2025.

question: Eric Arthur Blair was born in Motihari, Bihar. He went on to become famous as an author of a dystopian work which introduced the terms ‘Newspeak’, ‘Thoughtcrime’, and ‘Doublespeak’. He wrote under the pseudonym _______ .
infoBite: Orwell was born in Motihari in 1903. Nineteen Eighty-Four (1949) coined Newspeak, thoughtcrime, doublethink and Big Brother; Animal Farm appeared in 1945.
note: The paper says “Doublespeak”; the novel's own term is “doublethink”.

question:
“I started writing in Gikuyu language in 1977 after seventeen years of involvement in Afro-European literature, in my case Afro-English literature … wherever I have gone, particularly in Europe, I have been confronted with the question: why are you now writing in Gikuyu? Why do you now write in an African language?”
Identify the author of this passage.
infoBite: From Ngũgĩ's Decolonising the Mind (1986). In 1977 he co-wrote the Gikuyu play Ngaahika Ndeenda (I Will Marry When I Want); his novel Devil on the Cross (1980) was written in prison. Ngũgĩ was also asked in GATE 2025 and 2026.

question: On the basis of genre, which of the following does NOT belong in this group?

options.D: Ravan and Eddie by Kiran Nagarkar

infoBite: Ravan and Eddie (1995) is a novel; the others are plays — Harvest (1997, Onassis Prize), Tara (1990) and the Marathi Sakharam Binder (1972). Tara also appeared in GATE 2026.

question: The Madwoman in the Attic, the title of Sandra Gilbert and Susan Gubar’s iconic feminist examination of Victorian literature, alludes to which classic novel?
infoBite: The title points to Bertha Mason, Rochester's wife locked in the attic at Thornfield. Gilbert and Gubar's book appeared in 1979; Jean Rhys rewrote Bertha's story in Wide Sargasso Sea (1966).

question: Agatha Christie broke a fundamental rule of detective fiction in _______ .
infoBite: In The Murder of Roger Ackroyd (1926) the narrator, Dr James Sheppard, turns out to be the murderer — the classic unreliable-narrator twist.

question: Dorothea Brooke, Edward Casaubon, Hetty Sorel, Stephen Guest are all characters created by _______ .
infoBite: Dorothea and Casaubon are in Middlemarch (1871–72), Hetty Sorrel in Adam Bede (1859), and Stephen Guest in The Mill on the Floss (1860).
note: The paper spells the name “Sorel”; the novel has “Sorrel”.

question: Charulata is an adaptation of which work by Rabindranath Tagore?
infoBite: Satyajit Ray's film Charulata (1964) adapts Tagore's novella Nastanirh (1901). Ray also filmed The Home and the World as Ghare Baire (1984).

question: Which of the following is NOT part of the Theban trilogy?
infoBite: Sophocles' Theban plays are Oedipus Rex, Oedipus at Colonus and Antigone (written at different times, not as one trilogy). Medea (431 BCE) is by Euripides.

question: The literary term ‘apostrophe’ denotes:

options.A: A comparison of an abstract idea with its opposite.
options.B: An address to a person, or a personified idea or power.
options.C: A break within an iambic pentameter.
options.D: The possession of a character by a spirit.

infoBite: Apostrophe addresses an absent person or an abstraction as if present: “Death, be not proud” (Donne), “Milton! thou shouldst be living at this hour” (Wordsworth). A break within a line is a caesura.

question: In the line, “What’s Hecuba to him, or he to Hecuba?” “he” refers to _______ .

options.A: Virgil, the author of the Aeneid
options.B: An actor performing a scene from the Trojan War in Hamlet
options.C: Helen’s husband Priam who left her for Hecuba
options.D: A fairy king who abandoned his daughter Hecuba at birth

infoBite: From Hamlet's soliloquy “O, what a rogue and peasant slave am I!” (Act 2, Scene 2), after the First Player weeps reciting Aeneas's tale of Pyrrhus and Queen Hecuba.

question: Which of the following is/are NOT based on a play by William Shakespeare?

options.C: Girish Karnad’s The Fire and the Rain

infoBite: Pygmalion (1913) reworks Ovid's myth; The Fire and the Rain (Agni Mattu Male, 1995) draws on the Mahabharata's Yavakri story. Nutshell (2016) retells Hamlet from the womb; Throne of Blood (1957) is Kurosawa's Macbeth.

question: Which of the following is/are NOT composed by Kalidasa?
infoBite: Mṛcchakaṭika (The Little Clay Cart) is Śūdraka's; the Nāṭyaśāstra is Bharata's. Kālidāsa wrote Śākuntalam, Meghadūta, Raghuvaṃśa, Kumārasambhava, Mālavikāgnimitram and Vikramorvaśīyam.

question: Which of these writers is/are associated with the Progressive Writers Association?
infoBite: The Progressive Writers' Association held its first conference in Lucknow in 1936, presided over by Premchand; Sajjad Zaheer was a founder. Bankim died in 1894.

question: Which of the following novels is/are written by African-American women?
infoBite: The Color Purple (1982) won Alice Walker the Pulitzer; The Bluest Eye (1970) is Toni Morrison's first novel. The Ink Black Heart (2022) is by Robert Galbraith (J. K. Rowling); My Name Is Red (1998) is Orhan Pamuk's.

question: Which of the following options is NOT the title of a play?
infoBite: Scenes of Clerical Life (1858) is George Eliot's first fiction, three stories. The others are plays: Kyd's revenge tragedy (c. 1587), Ibsen's A Doll's House (1879), Brecht's Mother Courage (1939).
note: The paper prints “Scenes from Clerical Life”; Eliot's title is “Scenes of Clerical Life”.

question:
Match each fictional character with the author who created him:
a. Uriah Heep
b. Stephen Dedalus
c. Bazarov
d. Raskolnikov

i. James Joyce
ii. Ivan Turgenev
iii. Fyodor Dostoevsky
iv. Charles Dickens
works: A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man
infoBite: Uriah Heep: David Copperfield (1850); Stephen Dedalus: A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man (1916) and Ulysses; Bazarov, the nihilist: Fathers and Sons (1862); Raskolnikov: Crime and Punishment (1866).

question:
What do the following works have in common?
Andha Yug, The Second Turn, Parva, Sarpa Satra

options.B: All are based on the Mahabharata.
options.C: All have women as primary protagonists.

infoBite: Andha Yug (1954) is Dharamvir Bharati's Hindi verse play set at the war's end; Parva (1979) is S. L. Bhyrappa's Kannada novel; Sarpa Satra (2004) is Arun Kolatkar's poem on Janamejaya's snake sacrifice. Not all are plays, so A is out.
note: The author of “The Second Turn” isn't named in the paper and couldn't be confirmed, so it is left untagged.

question:
Match the texts with the language they were originally written in:
a. Waiting for a Visa
b. The Prisons we Broke
c. The Revenue Stamp: An Autobiography
d. Joothan: A Dalit’s Life

i. Hindi
ii. English
iii. Marathi
iv. Punjabi
infoBite: Ambedkar wrote Waiting for a Visa in English (c. 1935–36); Baby Kamble's Jina Amucha is Marathi; Amrita Pritam's Rasidi Ticket is Punjabi; Omprakash Valmiki's Joothan (1997) is Hindi.

question:
Match the excerpts with the texts they have been taken from:
a. “A son who will never be older than his motherland – neither older nor younger. There shall be two heads – but you will only see one – there will be knees and a nose, a nose and knees.”
b. “That it really began in the days when the Love Laws were made. The laws that lay down who should be loved, and how. And how much.”
c. “She had dispersed. She was the garden at Prem Niwas (soon to be entered into the annual Flower Show), she was Veena’s love of music, Pran’s asthma, Maan’s generosity, […] the temperament of Bhaskar’s great-grandchildren. Indeed, for all the Minister of Revenue’s impatience with her, she was his regret.”
d. “Two or three years after the 1947 Partition, it occurred to the governments of India and Pakistan to exchange their lunatics in the same manner as they had exchanged their criminals. The Muslim lunatics in India were to be sent over to Pakistan and the Hindu and Sikh lunatics in Pakistan asylums were to be handed over to India.”

i. A Suitable Boy
ii. Midnight’s Children
iii. The God of Small Things
iv. “Toba Tek Singh”
infoBite: a: the soothsayer Ramram Seth's prophecy of Saleem (Midnight's Children, 1981). b: the Love Laws (The God of Small Things, 1997). c: Mrs Mahesh Kapoor's death (A Suitable Boy, 1993). d: the opening of Manto's “Toba Tek Singh” (1955).

question: A widely used narrative technique, it allows narrators to temporarily inhabit the consciousness of any of their characters. It is called _______ .
infoBite: Free indirect speech (discourse) blends a character's thoughts into third-person narration without “she thought”. Austen, Flaubert and Woolf are standard examples; it was also asked in GATE 2026 with Mrs Dalloway.

question: Which of the following statements is true of Magic Realism?

options.A: It has its origins in the speech of the Oracle of Delphi.
options.B: It was created by J R R Tolkien.
options.C: It reveals the extraordinary in the heart of the ordinary.
options.D: It is a subset of Socialist Realism.

infoBite: Magic realism places marvels matter-of-factly inside realistic narrative. The term comes from Franz Roh's 1925 art criticism; García Márquez's One Hundred Years of Solitude (1967) and Rushdie's Midnight's Children are key examples.

question:
_______ wrote ‘Adonais: An Elegy on the Death of _______ .’
Fill in the blanks with the correct pair:
infoBite: Shelley wrote Adonais (1821), a pastoral elegy in 55 Spenserian stanzas, after Keats died in Rome in February 1821. Adonais was also asked in GATE 2026 as a pastoral elegy.

question: Which of the following statements about The Scarlet Letter is/are correct?

options.A: It was written by Nadine Gordimer.
options.B: The “scarlet letter” of the title refers to the letter ‘A’.
options.D: It was written in the 19th century.

infoBite: Hawthorne's The Scarlet Letter (1850): Hester Prynne wears an “A” for adultery in Puritan Boston. It opens with “The Custom-House” sketch and is not told in letters. Also asked in GATE 2026.

question:
“[…] I mean negative capability, that is when a man is capable of being in uncertainties, mysteries, doubts, without any irritable reaching after fact and reason […].”
Based on this statement, which of the following options is/are correct?
Negative capability is the ability to _______ .

options.C: not get irritated by people’s incompetence

works: Letter to George and Tom Keats (December 1817)
infoBite: From Keats's letter to his brothers George and Tom (December 1817), naming Shakespeare as the poet who had this quality “so enormously”. Keats contrasts it with Coleridge's restless reaching after knowledge.

question:
Virginia Woolf wrote in “Professions for Women”:
“You have won rooms of your own in the house hitherto exclusively owned by men. You are able, though not without great labour and effort, to pay the rent. You are earning your five hundred pounds a year. But this freedom is only a beginning; the room is your own, but it is still bare. It has to be furnished; it has to be decorated; it has to be shared. How are you going to furnish it, how are you going to decorate it? With whom are you going to share it, and upon what terms?”
Based on this passage, which of the following inferences is/are correct?

options.A: Women may have attained rooms of their own but they still have a long way to go.
options.B: The ‘room’ women now own is a sign of minimal economic independence.
options.C: Woolf insists that women live only with other women in order to maintain their independence.
options.D: The freedom that women now enjoy was attained after centuries of struggle.

infoBite: “Professions for Women” was a 1931 talk to the National Society for Women's Service, where Woolf describes killing the “Angel in the House” (Coventry Patmore's phrase). The room and £500 echo A Room of One's Own (1929).

question: Which of the following statements is/are correct?

options.A: Rasa is a form of categorizing a text by its genre.
options.B: According to Abhinavagupta, Rasa is best experienced collectively and in unison with others.
options.C: Rasa is purely an aesthetic emotion, not to be confused with real-life emotions.
options.D: Rasa is evoked only by performances like drama and dance.

infoBite: Abhinavagupta's Abhinavabhāratī, a commentary on Bharata's Nāṭyaśāstra, treats rasa as a generalised, impersonal relish (sādhāraṇīkaraṇa) enjoyed by the sahṛdaya, not a private real-life emotion. Rasa theory also came up in GATE 2025.

question:
“Lear cries out ‘you are men of stones’
as Cordelia hangs from a broken wall.
I step out into Chandni Chowk, a street once
strewn with jasmine flowers
for the Empress and the royal women
who bought perfumes from Isfahan,
fabrics from Dacca, essence from Kabul,
glass bangles from Agra.
Beggars now live here in tombs
of unknown nobles and forgotten saints
while hawkers sell combs and mirrors
outside a Sikh temple. Across the street,
a theater is showing a Bombay spectacular.
I think of Zafar, poet and Emperor,
being led through this street
by British soldiers, his feet in chains,
to watch his sons hanged.
In exile he wrote:
‘Unfortunate Zafar
spent half his life in hope,
the other half waiting.
He begs for two yards of Delhi for burial.’
He was exiled to Burma, buried in Rangoon.”
Which of the following ideas is/are conveyed by this poem?

options.A: Delhi is a modern and progressive city despite its imperial past.
options.B: Even Kings may be punished when they commit crimes against their children.
options.C: An exile’s sense of loss, and longing for their homeland.
options.D: History is a constant presence all around us.

infoBite: Bahadur Shah Zafar, the last Mughal emperor, was exiled to Rangoon after 1857 and died there in 1862; the lines echo his ghazal lament for “do gaz zameen” (two yards of earth). Lear's “men of stones” is from King Lear, Act 5, Scene 3.
note: The paper does not name the poem or poet, and the attribution couldn't be confirmed, so the poet is left untagged.

question:
Which of the following statements is/are true of these novels:
Anna Karenina, Dead Souls, Crime and Punishment, Fathers and Sons.

options.A: They are all written by Russian authors.
options.B: They all have women as central protagonists.
options.C: They were all written in the 19th century.
options.D: They all highlight socially transgressive romantic relationships.

infoBite: Dead Souls (Gogol, 1842), Fathers and Sons (Turgenev, 1862), Crime and Punishment (Dostoevsky, 1866), Anna Karenina (Tolstoy, 1877). Only Anna Karenina has a woman at its centre.

question:
“[…] in so far as the academic discourse of history – that is, ‘history’ as a discourse produced at the institutional site of the university – is concerned, ‘Europe’ remains the sovereign, theoretical subject of all histories, including the ones we call ‘Indian,’ ‘Chinese,’ ‘Kenyan,’ and so on. There is a peculiar way in which all these other histories tend to become variations on a master narrative that could be called ‘the history of Europe.’ In this sense, ‘Indian’ history itself is in a position of subalternity; one can only articulate subaltern subject positions in the name of this history.”
Which of the following options is/are implied by the passage above?

options.A: People in postcolonial societies are condemned to endlessly repeat their own histories.
options.B: The histories of India, China, and Kenya are not fundamentally different from one another.
options.C: Within the protocols of history writing, it is impossible to write the history of postcolonial societies without reference to Europe.
options.D: Instead of Europe, India should be the sovereign subject of all histories.

works: Postcoloniality and the Artifice of History
infoBite: From Dipesh Chakrabarty's “Postcoloniality and the Artifice of History” (1992), expanded in Provincializing Europe (2000). Chakrabarty belongs to the Subaltern Studies collective begun by Ranajit Guha.

question:
“What if, in order to save some humans lost in their language, in order to deliver the humans themselves, at the expense of their language, it was better to renounce the language, at least to renounce the best conditions for survival ‘at all costs’ for the idiom? And what if some humans were more worth saving than their language, under circumstances where, alas, one needed to choose between them? For we are living in a period in which the question at times arises. Today, on this earth of humans, certain people must yield to the homo-hegemony of dominant languages. They must learn the language of the masters, of capital and machines; they must lose their idiom in order to survive or live better.”
On the basis of this passage, which of the following options is/are correct?
The writer of this passage is:

options.A: Advocating that all colonized people should renounce their native languages to succeed in a globalized world.
options.B: Lamenting that in our contemporary world, some groups of people are forced to choose between immersion in their own language and economic survival.
options.C: Implicitly expressing despair about the hegemony of dominant languages.
options.D: Suggesting that there should be only one language in the world.

infoBite: The writer laments, rather than advocates, the pressure to give up one's idiom for the “language of the masters”. Compare Ngũgĩ's case for writing in Gikuyu (Q32 of this paper).
note: The paper does not name the source and the author couldn't be confirmed, so no writer is tagged.

question:
Politics — by William Butler Yeats
‘In our time the destiny of man presents its meanings in political terms.’ — Thomas Mann
“How can I, that girl standing there,
My attention fix
On Roman or on Russian
Or on Spanish politics,
Yet here’s a travelled man that knows
What he talks about,
And there’s a politician
That has both read and thought,
And maybe what they say is true
Of war and war’s alarms,
But O that I were young again
And held her in my arms.”
Which of the following options is/are implied by this poem?

options.A: Politics is the most absorbing concern of human existence.
options.B: Desire has never distracted the speaker from politics.
options.C: Sensual desire can be in conflict with cerebral concerns.
options.D: Physical desire does not die with age.

infoBite: “Politics” (1938) is among Yeats's last poems and closes Last Poems (1939). Its epigraph from Thomas Mann is answered with desire over public affairs. Yeats was also asked in GATE 2025.

question:
“Although feminist philosophers have traditionally sought to show how the body is figured as feminine, or how women have been associated with materiality (whether inert – always already dead – or fecund – ever-living and procreative) where men have been associated with the principle of rational mastery, Irigaray wants to argue that in fact the feminine is precisely what is excluded in and by such a binary opposition. In this sense, when and where women are represented within this economy is precisely the site of their erasure.”
Which of the following options is/are implied by this passage?

options.A: Irigaray’s work does not replicate the stance of traditional feminist philosophy.
options.B: Irigaray radically questions the mind/body distinction from a feminist perspective.
options.C: For Irigaray, the place assigned to women, even by some feminist philosophers, may in fact serve to erase them.
options.D: Irigaray is not crucially concerned about the feminine.

works: This Sex Which Is Not One
infoBite: Luce Irigaray, with Hélène Cixous and Julia Kristeva, is a key French feminist; her major works are Speculum of the Other Woman (1974) and This Sex Which Is Not One (1977).

question:
“I like a look of Agony,
Because I know it’s true –
Men do not sham Convulsion,
Nor simulate, a Throe –
The eyes glaze once – and that is Death –
Impossible to feign
The Beads upon the Forehead
By homely Anguish strung.”
Which of the following options is/are implied by this poem?

options.B: The speaker likes to watch people suffer because it reminds her of her own wellbeing.
options.C: Strong people never suffer a painful death.

works: I like a look of Agony
infoBite: Emily Dickinson's poem (c. 1861) values agony because it cannot be faked. Note her dashes, capitalised nouns and slant rhyme; most of her poems were published only after her death in 1886.

question:
“We dwell with satisfaction upon the poet’s difference from his predecessors, especially his immediate predecessors; […]. Whereas if we approach a poet without this prejudice we shall often find that not only the best, but the most individual parts of his works may be those in which the dead poets, his ancestors, assert their immortality most vigorously.”
Which of the following options is/are implied by this excerpt?

options.A: Being different from one’s predecessors need not be the defining characteristic of a good poet.
options.B: What we consider original in a poem, may be deeply rooted in tradition.
options.C: There is no difference between old and new poems.
options.D: The past is often a living presence in good contemporary poetry.

infoBite: From T. S. Eliot's “Tradition and the Individual Talent” (1919), on the “historical sense”. The same essay supplied GATE 2026's “escape from personality” passage, so read it whole.

question: Which factor(s) led to the rise and popularity of the novel in England?

options.B: The spread of printing presses throughout England.
options.C: The migration of large numbers of writers and intellectuals from Italy.

infoBite: Ian Watt's The Rise of the Novel (1957) links the form to a growing literate middle-class readership, print culture and circulating libraries, with Defoe, Richardson and Fielding as the founders.

question:
Rafi told Mary, “I am thinking of watching a film this weekend.”
The following reports the above statement in indirect speech:
Rafi told Mary that he _______ of watching a film that weekend.
infoBite: After a past reporting verb (“told”), present continuous shifts back to past continuous: “am thinking” → “was thinking”, and “this weekend” → “that weekend”.

question:
Permit : _______ : : Enforce : Relax
(By word meaning)
infoBite: “Enforce” and “relax” are opposites, so “permit” pairs with its opposite, “forbid”.

question: Given a fair six-faced dice where the faces are labelled ‘1’, ‘2’, ‘3’, ‘4’, ‘5’, and ‘6’, what is the probability of getting a ‘1’ on the first roll of the dice and a ‘4’ on the second roll?
infoBite: The two rolls are independent, so multiply: 1/6 × 1/6 = 1/36.

question:
A recent survey shows that 65% of tobacco users were advised to stop consuming tobacco. The survey also shows that 3 out of 10 tobacco users attempted to stop using tobacco.
Based only on the information in the above passage, which one of the following options can be logically inferred with certainty?

options.A: A majority of tobacco users who were advised to stop consuming tobacco made an attempt to do so.
options.B: A majority of tobacco users who were advised to stop consuming tobacco did not attempt to do so.
options.C: Approximately 30% of tobacco users successfully stopped consuming tobacco.
options.D: Approximately 65% of tobacco users successfully stopped consuming tobacco.

infoBite: 65 in 100 were advised but only 30 in 100 tried, so even if every one who tried had been advised, fewer than half of the advised attempted. Nothing is said about success, so C and D can't be inferred.

question:
Students of all the departments of a college who have successfully completed the registration process are eligible to vote in the upcoming college elections. However, by the time the due date for registration was over, it was found that suprisingly none of the students from the Department of Human Sciences had completed the registration process.
Based only on the information provided above, which one of the following sets of statement(s) can be logically inferred with certainty?
(i) All those students who would not be eligible to vote in the college elections would certainly belong to the Department of Human Sciences.
(ii) None of the students from departments other than Human Sciences failed to complete the registration process within the due time.
(iii) All the eligible voters would certainly be students who are not from the Department of Human Sciences.
infoBite: Only registered students can vote and no Human Sciences student registered, so every eligible voter is from another department (iii). (i) and (ii) assume everyone else registered, which isn't stated.

question:
Which one of the options does NOT describe the passage below or follow from it?
We tend to think of cancer as a ‘modern’ illness because its metaphors are so modern. It is a disease of overproduction, of sudden growth, a growth that is unstoppable, tipped into the abyss of no control. Modern cell biology encourages us to imagine the cell as a molecular machine. Cancer is that machine unable to quench its intial command (to grow) and thus transform into an indestructible, self-propelled automaton.
[Adapted from The Emperor of All Maladies by Siddhartha Mukherjee]

options.A: It is a reflection of why cancer seems so modern to most of us.
options.B: It tells us that modern cell biology uses and promotes metaphors of machinery.
options.C: Modern cell biology encourages metaphors of machinery, and cancer is often imagined as a machine.
options.D: Modern cell biology never uses figurative language, such as metaphors, to describe or explain anything.

infoBite: The passage itself shows cell biology using a machine metaphor, so D contradicts it. Mukherjee's The Emperor of All Maladies (2010) won the 2011 Pulitzer Prize for General Nonfiction.

question: The digit in the unit’s place of the product 3^999 × 7^1000 is _______.
infoBite: Last digits of powers of 3 cycle 3, 9, 7, 1 and of 7 cycle 7, 9, 3, 1. 999 leaves remainder 3 when divided by 4, so 3^999 ends in 7; 7^1000 ends in 1. 7 × 1 = 7.
note: Exponents are typeset in the original; written here with ^.

question: Which word below best describes the idea of being both Spineless and Cowardly?
infoBite: Pusillanimous = timid, lacking courage. Unctuous = oily and flattering; obsequious = too eager to please; reticent = reserved, saying little.

question:
Choose the right preposition to fill up the blank:
The whole family got together ___ Diwali
infoBite: Use “at” for a festival or holiday period (at Diwali, at Christmas) and “on” for the particular day (on Diwali day).

question:
Select the correct option to fill in all the blanks to complete the passage:
The (i)_______ factor amid this turbulence has been the (ii)________ of high-octane, action-oriented films such as RRR, K.G.F: Chapter 2 and Pushpa from film industries in the south of the country. Traditionally, films made in the south have done well in their own (iii) _________. But increasingly, their dubbed versions have performed well in the Hindi heartland, with collections (iv)________ those of their Bollywood counterparts.
infoBite: “Amid this turbulence” plus “performed well” signals a positive turn: the redeeming factor was the southern films' outperformance, with collections eclipsing Bollywood's.

question:
The following passage consists of 6 sentences. The first and sixth sentences of the passage are at their correct positions, while the middle four sentences (represented by 2, 3, 4, and 5) are jumbled up.
Choose the correct sequence of the sentences so that they form a coherent paragraph:
1. Most obviously, mobility is taken to be a geographical as well as a social phenomenon.
2. Much of the social mobility literature regarded society as a uniform surface and failed to register the geographical intersections of region, city and place, with the social categories of class, gender and ethnicity.
3. The existing sociology of migration is incidentally far too limited in its concerns to be very useful here.
4. Further, I am concerned with the flows of people within, but especially beyond, the territory of each society, and how these flows may relate to many different desires, for work, housing, leisure, religion, family relationships, criminal gain, asylum seeking and so on.
5. Moreover, not only people are mobile but so too are many ‘objects’.
6. I show that sociology’s recent development of a ‘sociology of objects’ needs to be taken further and that the diverse flows of objects across societal borders and their intersections with the multiple flows of people are hugely significant.
infoBite: Sentence 2 explains “geographical as well as social”, 3 adds an aside on migration studies, “Further” (4) adds the next concern, and “Moreover… objects” (5) leads into 6 on the sociology of objects.

question: The population of a country increased by 5% from 2020 to 2021. Then, the population decreased by 5% from 2021 to 2022. By what percentage did the population change from 2020 to 2022?
infoBite: 1.05 × 0.95 = 0.9975, a net fall of 0.25%. An equal percentage rise and fall never cancel out.

question: The words Thin: Slim: Slender are related in some way. Identify the correct option(s) that reflect(s) the same relationship:
infoBite: Thin, slim and slender name the same quality in increasingly flattering words; so do fat/plump/voluptuous and short/small/petite. Tall/taller/tallest is degrees of comparison.

question:
A pandemic like situation hit the country last year, resulting in loss of human life and economic depression. To improve the condition of its citizens, the government made a series of emergency medical interventions and increased spending to revive the economy. In both these efforts, district administration authorities were actively involved.
Which of the following action(s) are plausible?

options.A: In future, the government can make district administration authorities responsible for protecting health of citizens and reviving the economy.
options.B: The government may set up a task force to review the post pandemic situation and ascertain the effectiveness of the measures taken.
options.C: The government may set up a committee to formulate a pandemic management program to minimize losses to life and economy in future.
options.D: The government may take population control measures to minimize pandemic related losses in future.

infoBite: Reviewing what worked and planning for the next pandemic follow from the situation. Making districts solely responsible, or population control, doesn't.

question: Six students, Arif, Balwinder, Chintu, David, Emon and Fulmoni appeared in the GATE-XH exam in 2022. Balwinder scores less than Chintu in XH-B1, but more than Arif in XH-C1. David scores more than Balwinder in XH-C1, and more than Chintu in XH-B1. Emon scores less than David, but more than Fulmoni in XH-B1. Fulmoni scores more than David in XH-C1. Arif scores less than Emon, but more than Fulmoni in XH-B1. Who scores highest in XH-B1?
infoBite: Use only the XH-B1 clues: David > Chintu > Balwinder and David > Emon > Arif > Fulmoni, so David is highest. The XH-C1 clues are distractors.

question:
Select the correct relation between E and F.
E = x/(1+x) and F = −x/(1−x), x > 1
infoBite: For x > 1, E = x/(1+x) is less than 1, while F = −x/(1−x) = x/(x−1) is more than 1. So E < F.

question:
A code language is formulated thus:
Vowels in the original word are replaced by the next vowel from the list of vowels, A-E-I-O-U (For example, E is replaced by I and U is replaced by A). Consonants in the original word are replaced by previous consonant (For example, T is replaced by S and V is replaced by T).
Then how does the word, GOODMORNING appear in the coded language?
infoBite: G→F, O→U, O→U, D→C, M→L, O→U, R→Q, N→M, I→O, N→M, G→F: FUUCLUQMOMF.

question:
The stranger is by nature no "owner of soil" -- soil not only in the physical, but also in the figurative sense of a life-substance, which is fixed, if not in a point in space, at least in an ideal point of the social environment. Although in more intimate relations, he may develop all kinds of charm and significance, as long as he is considered a stranger in the eyes of the other, he is not an "owner of soil." Restriction to intermediary trade, and often (as though sublimated from it) to pure finance, gives him the specific character of mobility. If mobility takes place within a closed group, it embodies that synthesis of nearness and distance which constitutes the formal position of the stranger. For, the fundamentally mobile person comes in contact, at one time or another, with every individual, but is not organically connected, through established ties of kinship, locality, and occupation, with any single one.
What assumptions can be made about the stranger from the passage above?

options.A: The stranger can become an owner of soil through developing all kinds of charm in more intimate relations.
options.B: The stranger cannot become an owner of soil either in the physical or psychological sense.
options.C: The stranger can become an owner of soil through establishing ties of kinship and so on.
options.D: The stranger might become an owner of soil in the physical sense but not in the psychological

infoBite: Adapted from Georg Simmel's essay “The Stranger” (1908): the stranger combines nearness and distance and has no organic ties, so he owns “soil” in neither sense.

question:
L is the only son of A and S. S has one sibling, B, who is married to L’s aunt, K. B is the only son of D. How are L and D related?
Select the possible option(s):
infoBite: B is D's only son, so B's sibling S must be a daughter, i.e. L's mother. D is L's maternal grandparent; D's gender isn't given, so both B and D.

question:
Five segments of a sentence are given below. The first and fifth segments are at their correct positions, while the middle three segments (represented by 2, 3, and 4) are jumbled up. Choose the correct order of the segments so that they form a coherent sentence:
1. Consumed multitudes are jostling and shoving inside me
2. and guided only by the memory of a large white bedsheet with a roughly circular hole some seven inches in diameter cut into the center,
3. clutching at the dream of that holey, mutilated square of linen, which is my talisman, my open-sesame,
4. I must commence the business of remaking my life from the point at which it really began,
5. some thirty-two years before anything as obvious, as present, as my clock-ridden, crime-stained birth.
infoBite: The sentence is from the first chapter of Rushdie's Midnight's Children (1981), “The Perforated Sheet” — the sheet through which Aadam Aziz first examined Naseem.

question:
“I told you the truth,” I say yet again, “Memory’s truth, because memory has its own special kind. It selects, eliminates, alters, exaggerates, minimizes, glorifies, and vilifies also; but in the end it creates its own reality, its heterogeneous but usually coherent versions of events; and no sane human being ever trusts someone else’s version more than his own.”
What are the different ways in which ‘truth’ can be understood from the passage?

options.A: Truth is what can be verified by hard empirical evidence.
options.B: Truth is based on what can be perceived by the senses.
options.C: Truth is the product of memory that is fallible, selective and slanted.
options.D: Truth is contingent on the observer and can only be partial.

infoBite: Saleem Sinai defends “memory's truth” to Padma in Midnight's Children — a key statement of the novel's unreliable narration. Midnight's Children also appears in Q23 and Q62 of this paper.

question: A firm needs both skilled labour and unskilled labour for the production of cloth. The wage of skilled labour is Rs. 40,000 per month, and that of unskilled labour is Rs. 15,000 per month. The total wage bill of the firm for the production of cloth is Rs. 23,75,000 in a month for 100 labour. How many skilled labour are employed by the firm (in Integer)?

Select the odd word and write the option number as answer:
(1) Lek (2) Zloty (3) Diner (4) Drachma (5) Real
infoBite: Lek (Albania), złoty (Poland), drachma (Greece, before the euro) and real (Brazil) are currencies. “Diner” is not — the currency is the dinar.

question: Who published the novel The Bell Jar under the pseudonym Victoria Lucas?
infoBite: The Bell Jar came out in January 1963 as by “Victoria Lucas”, a month before Plath's death; it appeared under her own name in 1966. Pseudonyms were also asked in GATE 2024 (Orwell).

question: In which collection did Walt Whitman’s poem “Song of Myself” first appear?
infoBite: “Song of Myself” opened the first edition of Leaves of Grass (1855) without a title; it got its final title in 1881. The Golden Bough is J. G. Frazer's study of myth and ritual.

question: Who wrote the introduction to Rabindranath Tagore’s Gitanjali?
infoBite: Yeats introduced Gitanjali: Song Offerings (London, 1912). Tagore won the Nobel Prize in 1913, the first non-European laureate.

question:
Identify the title of the poem in which the following lines appear:
“He was found by the Bureau of Statistics to be
One against whom there was no official complaint,
And all the reports on his conduct agree
That, in the modern sense of an old-fashioned word, he was a saint
For in everything he did he served the greater community.”
works: In Memory of W. B. Yeats
infoBite: Auden's satire on the conforming, statistically perfect citizen (1939), collected in Another Time (1940). All four options are Auden poems; Q53 of this paper quotes the Yeats elegy.

question:
Identify the point of view used in the following passage:
“You are not the kind of guy who would be at a place like this at this time of the morning. But here you are, and you cannot say that the terrain is entirely unfamiliar, though the details are fuzzy.”
infoBite: Second-person narration addresses the protagonist as “you”. The passage opens Jay McInerney's Bright Lights, Big City (1984); Calvino's If on a Winter's Night a Traveller (Q64) also uses it.

question: Which of the following is a novel by Charles Dickens?
infoBite: The Old Curiosity Shop (1840–41) follows Little Nell. The Old Wives' Tale (1908) is Arnold Bennett's; The Old Bachelor (1693) is Congreve's first comedy.

question:
Which linguistic process can be seen in the formation of the following words?
i. smog, ii. brunch, iii. motel iv. telecast
infoBite: Blends fuse parts of two words: smoke + fog, breakfast + lunch, motor + hotel, television + broadcast. Backformation removes a supposed affix (edit from editor).

question: Which writer is credited with the ‘chutneyfication’ of Indian English?
infoBite: In Midnight's Children (1981) Saleem, who works in a pickle factory, speaks of the “chutnification of history”; the term is now used for Rushdie's hybrid, Hindi-laced English.

question: Whom would you associate the term ‘simulacra’ with?
infoBite: Baudrillard's Simulacra and Simulation (1981) describes hyperreality, where copies without originals replace the real.

question: In Plato’s idea of the Republic there is no place for the ___________.
infoBite: In the Republic (Books III and X) Plato banishes poets: poetry imitates an imitation, “thrice removed” from truth, and stirs the passions. Aristotle's Poetics answers him.

question: What was Aristotle’s definition of hubris?

options.B: A false sense of pride which eventually causes the character’s downfall
options.C: An ability to imagine the future

infoBite: Hubris is overweening pride that leads the hero to defy the gods or moral order. Don't confuse it with hamartia (“error of judgement”, option A's “tragic flaw”), the term Aristotle uses in the Poetics.
note: The Poetics itself names hamartia, not hubris; the official key accepts B as the standard definition.

question: Stephen Dedalus is a recurring character in the works of _________.
works: A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man
infoBite: Stephen Dedalus appears in Stephen Hero, A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man (1916) and Ulysses (1922). He was asked again in GATE 2024.

question: Which of the following novels opens with the sentence, “It is a truth universally acknowledged that a single man in possession of a good fortune must be in want of a wife.”?
infoBite: The ironic opening of Pride and Prejudice (1813), first drafted as “First Impressions”. All four options are Austen novels.

question: Which of the following novels by Chinua Achebe derives its title from W. B. Yeats’s poem “The Second Coming”?
infoBite: “Things fall apart; the centre cannot hold” is from “The Second Coming” (1920). No Longer at Ease (1960) takes its title from Eliot's “Journey of the Magi”. Things Fall Apart was also asked in GATE 2026.

question: Identify the novels that deal with the trauma of Partition:

options.A: Shauna Singh Baldwin’s What the Body Remembers
options.D: Kamala Markandaya’s Nectar in a Sieve

infoBite: What the Body Remembers (1999) follows two Sikh women up to Partition; The Shadow Lines (1988) ties Partition to the 1964 riots in Dhaka and Calcutta. Cry, the Peacock (1963) is psychological; Nectar in a Sieve (1954) is about rural poverty.

question: Which of the following writers are associated with the Theatre of the Absurd?
infoBite: Martin Esslin coined the label in The Theatre of the Absurd (1961): Beckett, Ionesco, Genet, Pinter (The Birthday Party), Albee (The Zoo Story). Osborne was an “Angry Young Man”.

question: Identify the writers who are referred to as ‘metaphysical poets’:
infoBite: Samuel Johnson fixed the label in his Life of Cowley (1779). Eliot championed them in “The Metaphysical Poets” (1921) but wasn't one; Larkin is a Movement poet (asked in GATE 2026).

question: What are the sources of Girish Karnad’s Hayavadana?
infoBite: Hayavadana (1971) reworks the transposed-heads tale of the Vetālapañcaviṃśati in Somadeva's Kathāsaritsāgara, via Thomas Mann's novella The Transposed Heads (1940), using Yakshagana conventions.
note: The paper prints “Transported Heads”; Mann's title in English is The Transposed Heads.

question: Which of the following terms are used by Samuel Taylor Coleridge in his theory of imagination?

options.A: Primary imagination, secondary imagination, and fancy

infoBite: Biographia Literaria, ch. XIII (1817). The distractors mix Keats (negative capability; “egotistical sublime” for Wordsworth), Arnold (Hellenism), Eliot (impersonality), Emerson (oversoul) and Shelley (“unacknowledged legislators”). Also asked in GATE 2025.

question: Which of the following is the forerunner of the autobiography?

options.B: James Joyce’s Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man

works: A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man
infoBite: Augustine's Confessions (c. 397–400 CE) is usually called the first Western autobiography. Walton's Lives are biographies; The Prelude is autobiographical verse; Portrait is a Künstlerroman.

question: Which of the following poems did Robert Browning intend to write as a play?
infoBite: The Inn Album (1875) is a melodramatic verse narrative. Men and Women (1855) and Dramatis Personae (1864) are collections of monologues; The Ring and the Book (1868–69) is a 12-book poem of monologues.
note: Answer follows the official key; the claim that it began as a planned play couldn't be confirmed independently.

question: The ‘Age of Reason’ in English literary history is popularly known as:
infoBite: The Neoclassical Age (c. 1660–1798, from the Restoration to Lyrical Ballads) prized reason, order and decorum: Dryden, Pope, Swift, Johnson.

question: Who first translated Jacques Derrida’s work into English?
infoBite: Spivak's translation of Of Grammatology (1976), with her long Translator's Preface, made Derrida widely known in English.
note: David B. Allison's translation of Speech and Phenomena (1973) came earlier; the official key credits Spivak.

question: Identify the ‘Lake Poets’:
infoBite: Named for the Lake District, the label began as a sneer in the Edinburgh Review. Southey became Poet Laureate in 1813; Byron mocks him in the dedication of Don Juan.

question: Choose from the following options the type of drama that is intended by the author to be read rather than to be performed:
infoBite: Closet drama is meant to be read: Milton's Samson Agonistes, Byron's Manfred, Shelley's Prometheus Unbound. Kitchen-sink drama is 1950s British realism (Look Back in Anger).

question: Identify the commonality shared by the authors of Mansfield Park and Middle March:

options.A: Both the novels were authored by men who were sent on exile.
options.B: Both the novels were authored by political prisoners.
options.C: Both the novels were written by children who were not allowed to publish their works.
options.D: Both the novels were written by women who wrote under pseudonyms.

infoBite: George Eliot was Mary Ann Evans (Middlemarch, 1871–72). Austen published anonymously — Mansfield Park (1814) appeared as “by the author of Sense and Pride and Prejudice”.
note: The key's “pseudonyms” is loose for Austen, who was anonymous rather than pseudonymous; D is still the only possible option.

question: Who said, “Poetry makes nothing happen”?
works: In Memory of W. B. Yeats
infoBite: From Part II of Auden's “In Memory of W. B. Yeats” (1939): poetry changes nothing, yet it survives as a way of happening. Auden also appears in Q30.

question:
Which literary device does the following line employ?
“A timorous foe, and a suspicious friend.”
infoBite: Antithesis sets contrasting ideas in parallel phrases. The line is from Pope's portrait of Atticus (Addison) in Epistle to Dr Arbuthnot (1735). An oxymoron joins contradictory words directly.

question:
Match the following excerpts with their authors:
(P) “He rose from the table; and advancing to the master, basin and spoon in hand, said: somewhat alarmed at his own temerity: ‘Please, Sir, I want some more’.”
(Q) “Studies serve for delight, for ornament, and for ability.”
(R) “Trust thyself: every heart vibrates to that iron string.”
(S) “It was a bright cold day in April, and the clocks were striking thirteen.”

(i) Ralph Waldo Emerson
(ii) George Orwell
(iii) Charles Dickens
(iv) Francis Bacon
infoBite: P: Oliver Twist (1837–39), ch. 2. Q: Bacon's essay “Of Studies” (1597). R: Emerson's “Self-Reliance” (1841). S: the opening line of Nineteen Eighty-Four (1949).

question: The 1667 edition of Paradise Lost had 10 books. How many more were added to the 1674 edition?
infoBite: For the 1674 edition Milton split Books 7 and 10, making 12 books on the model of Virgil's Aeneid.
note: Marked MSQ in the official key with a single correct answer, A.

question:
Read the following poem and identify the appropriate options:
And search
for certain thin –
stemmed, bubble-eyed water bugs.
See them perch
on dry capillary legs
weightless
on the ripple skin
of a stream.
No, not only prophets
walk on water. This bug sits
on a landslide of lights
and drowns eye –
deep
into its tiny strip
of sky.

options.D: It juxtaposes the non-human with the human.

infoBite: No set metre or rhyme (free verse), precise visual images, and the bug set beside “prophets” who walk on water — the non-human placed against the human.
note: The paper doesn't name the poem and the poet couldn't be confirmed, so no writer is tagged.

question: Which of the following employ ‘Interior Monologue’?

options.B: The final chapter of James Joyce’s Ulysses
options.C: T. S. Eliot’s “The Love Song of J. Alfred Prufrock”

works: The Love Song of J. Alfred Prufrock
infoBite: Molly Bloom's unpunctuated “Penelope” episode ending Ulysses is the classic interior monologue; the key also counts Prufrock's inner musing. “My Last Duchess” is spoken aloud to a listener (dramatic monologue).

question: Which of the following works may be described as novels in verse?

options.A: Aurora Leigh by Elizabeth Barrett Browning
options.B: The Golden Gate by Vikram Seth
options.D: Old Possum’s Book of Practical Cats by T. S. Eliot

works: Old Possum's Book of Practical Cats
infoBite: Aurora Leigh (1856) is a nine-book blank-verse novel; The Golden Gate (1986) is told in 590 tetrameter sonnets after Pushkin's Eugene Onegin. Pamela (1740) is an epistolary prose novel.

question: Which of the following critics belong to the deconstructionist school?
infoBite: De Man and Hillis Miller (with Geoffrey Hartman and Harold Bloom) formed the “Yale School” that brought Derrida's deconstruction to American criticism. Kate Soper is a philosopher of nature and ecology.

question: Cleanth Brooks’s definition of ‘paradox’ in poetry foregrounds the following qualities:

options.D: Omniscience and death of the author

infoBite: In “The Language of Paradox” (The Well Wrought Urn, 1947) Brooks calls paradox the language of poetry, working through wonder and irony; his key example is Donne's “The Canonization”.

question: Two examples of magic realist fiction include:
infoBite: Rushdie's Midnight's Children (1981) and Grass's The Tin Drum (1959), whose Oskar refuses to grow, mix the marvellous with history. The English Teacher (1945) is realist; Tom Jones (1749) is a comic novel. Magic realism was also asked in GATE 2024.

question: Ferdinand de Saussure differentiates language in terms of:
infoBite: Course in General Linguistics (1916, compiled after his death from students' notes): langue is the shared system, parole the individual utterance. Metaphor/metonymy is Roman Jakobson's pair.

question: Which of the following are considered to be typical postmodern narratives?

options.A: Italo Calvino’s If on a Winter’s Night a Traveller
options.B: John Barth’s Lost in the Funhouse

works: If on a Winter's Night a Traveller
infoBite: If on a Winter's Night a Traveller (1979), Lost in the Funhouse (1968) and V. (1963) are metafictional postmodern classics. Murdoch's The Bell (1958) is a realist novel.

question: What does a green reading of a text aim at?

options.A: Analyzing the implications of a text for environmental concerns
options.C: Studying connections between humans, society and the non-human world

infoBite: Ecocriticism studies literature and the physical environment; Cheryll Glotfelty's The Ecocriticism Reader (1996) gives the standard definition. It questions the human/non-human divide.

question: Inhaling the smoke from a burning _________ could _________ you quickly.
infoBite: British “tyre” is the rubber wheel cover; the verb “tire” means to make weary. A “tier” is a row or level.

question:
A sphere of radius r cm is packed in a box of cubical shape.
What should be the minimum volume (in cm³) of the box that can enclose the sphere?
infoBite: The smallest cube has side equal to the sphere's diameter, 2r, so its volume is (2r)³ = 8r³.
note: Powers are typeset in the original; written here with ³.

question:
Pipes P and Q can fill a storage tank in full with water in 10 and 6 minutes, respectively. Pipe R draws the water out from the storage tank at a rate of 34 litres per minute. P, Q and R operate at a constant rate.
If it takes one hour to completely empty a full storage tank with all the pipes operating simultaneously, what is the capacity of the storage tank (in litres)?
infoBite: Net outflow per minute is 34 − V/10 − V/6, and it must equal V/60. So 34 = 17V/60, giving V = 120 litres.

question:
Six persons P, Q, R, S, T and U are sitting around a circular table facing the center not necessarily in the same order. Consider the following statements:
• P sits next to S and T.
• Q sits diametrically opposite to P.
• The shortest distance between S and R is equal to the shortest distance between T and U.
Based on the above statements, Q is a neighbor of
infoBite: With P between S and T and Q opposite P, the two seats beside Q go to R and U; the equal-distance clue puts R next to S's side and U next to T's.

question:
Rice, a versatile and inexpensive source of carbohydrate, is a critical component of diet worldwide. Climate change, causing extreme weather, poses a threat to sustained availability of rice. Scientists are working on developing Green Super Rice (GSR), which is resilient under extreme weather conditions yet gives higher yields sustainably.
Which one of the following is the CORRECT logical inference based on the information given in the above passage?

options.A: GSR is an alternative to regular rice, but it grows only in an extreme weather
options.B: GSR may be used in future in response to adverse effects of climate change
options.C: GSR grows in an extreme weather, but the quantity of produce is lesser than regular rice
options.D: Regular rice will continue to provide good yields even in extreme weather

infoBite: GSR is still being developed and is built to withstand extreme weather with high yields, so it may be used in future. “Only” in extreme weather and “lower yield” contradict the passage.

question:
A game consists of spinning an arrow around a stationary disk. When the arrow comes to rest, there are eight equally likely outcomes. It could come to rest in any one of the sectors numbered 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7 or 8.
Two such disks are used in a game where their arrows are independently spun.
What is the probability that the sum of the numbers on the resulting sectors upon spinning the two disks is equal to 8 after the arrows come to rest?
infoBite: There are 8 × 8 = 64 outcomes. Pairs adding to 8 are (1,7), (2,6), (3,5), (4,4), (5,3), (6,2), (7,1) — 7 of them, so 7/64.
note: The original shows a picture of the numbered disk; the text is enough to solve it.

question:
Consider the following inequalities.
(i) 3p − q < 4
(ii) 3q − p < 12
Which one of the following expressions below satisfies the above two inequalities?
infoBite: Add the two inequalities: 2p + 2q < 16, so p + q < 8.

question:
Given below are three statements and four conclusions drawn based on the statements.
Statement 1: Some engineers are writers.
Statement 2: No writer is an actor.
Statement 3: All actors are engineers.
Conclusion I: Some writers are engineers.
Conclusion II: All engineers are actors.
Conclusion III: No actor is a writer.
Conclusion IV: Some actors are writers.
Which one of the following options can be logically inferred?

options.B: Only conclusion II and conclusion III are correct
options.C: Only conclusion I and conclusion III are correct
options.D: Either conclusion III or conclusion IV is correct

infoBite: I is the converse of statement 1 and III restates statement 2. “All actors are engineers” does not make all engineers actors.

question:
A relationship is expressed as Iodine : Goitre.
The pair(s) of words showing SIMILAR relationship is/are
infoBite: Goitre comes from a lack of iodine, as diabetes involves a lack (or poor use) of insulin. Fat causes obesity by excess, the opposite relation.

question:
Three individuals are named P, Q, and R. Together they have a total of fifteen children of which nine are boys. P has three girls and Q has same number of boys. Q has one more child than P, who has four children. R has four more boys than the number of girls. The number of girls of R is equal to the number of boys of P.
How many boys do R and P have?
infoBite: P has 4 children with 3 girls, so 1 boy. R's girls = P's boys = 1, so R has 1 + 4 = 5 boys.

question:
A sentence has been given below.
The train will leave at 8:30 PM, we [have been] ready by 7:30 PM, so that we can reach the station on time.
To make the above sentence grammatically correct, the phrase marked in bold (shown here in brackets) is to be replaced by
infoBite: A future obligation needs a modal: “we must be ready by 7:30 PM”. “Have been” wrongly puts a future plan in the present perfect.
note: The paper shows the phrase in bold; it is marked here with brackets. Reading the bolded words as “have been” follows from the key.

question:
Complete the sentence correctly using the options given below.
Hastings____(p)_____ developed as a holiday resort after ___(q)____ .

options.A: (p) = a seaside town, (q) = the first world war
options.B: (p) = , a seaside town, (q) = the First World War
options.C: (p) = , a Seaside Town, (q) = World War I
options.D: (p) = A seaside town (q) = World War I

infoBite: An appositive (“a seaside town”) is set off by commas, and the name of the war takes capitals: “the First World War”.

question:
The Arecibo telescope does not resemble what most of us think of when we hear the word telescope. Its reflective surface covers an area of 20 acres, which is quite remarkable. Dangling above it are towers and cables, sub-reflectors and antennas, all of which can be positioned using 26 motors to transmit radio waves and receive echoes with astonishing precision.
From the passage, it can be inferred that most telescopes

options.A: are not as large as Arecibo

infoBite: Calling its 20-acre surface “remarkable” and unlike what we picture implies ordinary telescopes are much smaller.

question:
Tailgating another vehicle is unsafe and illegal. Many rear-end collisions are caused by drivers following too close to the vehicle in front of them. The rules state that a driver must keep significant distance from the vehicle in front in order to stop safely and avoid a collision. Drivers should allow a minimum two seconds gap between their vehicle and the one ahead. At 60 km per hour, this equates to a gap of 33 meters; at 100 km per hour, it equates to a gap of 55 meters. More distance is needed to safely stop in rain or poor visibility, as during rain slippery roads reduce the effectiveness of braking.
Which of the following statement(s) can be inferred from the above passage?

options.A: People drive faster in rain and under poor visibility.
options.B: Braking may not be as effective during rain as in the dry conditions.
options.C: Tailgating is against the road rules.
options.D: Collision has no relationship with tailgating.

infoBite: The passage calls tailgating illegal and says slippery roads reduce braking. Nothing says people drive faster in rain, and it directly links tailgating to collisions.

question: There are three separate, but equal-sized boxes. Inside each box, there are two separate small boxes. Inside each of the small boxes, there are four even smaller boxes. The total number of boxes will be _______ .

In a specific language, xer dan means “big horse”, liro cas means “red tomato” and dum cas dan means “big red barn”.
The equivalent word for barn in this language is
infoBite: “dan” is common to big horse and big red barn, so dan = big; “cas” is common to the red items, so cas = red. That leaves dum = barn.

question:
Park street is parallel to Rock street. Garden street is perpendicular (90°) to Lake street. Lake street is parallel to Rock street.
For the situation described above, the TRUE statement is

options.A: Park street is perpendicular to Lake street
options.B: Rock street is parallel to Garden street
options.C: Park street is parallel to Garden street
options.D: Garden street is perpendicular to Park street

infoBite: Park, Rock and Lake are all parallel. Garden is perpendicular to Lake, so it is perpendicular to Park too.

question: Six examinations are required to be conducted in a week starting from Sunday to Saturday. Hindi is not scheduled on the first day and English is not scheduled before Hindi. Mathematics is scheduled one day after Physics. Biology is scheduled two days after Hindi. One day prior to Chemistry, there is no examination. Only one examination can be scheduled on a single day and Sunday is not an off day. What are the subjects scheduled on first and the last days?

options.A: First day Physics, Last day Biology
options.B: First day Physics, Last day Chemistry
options.C: First day Physics, Last day English
options.D: First day English, Last day Biology

infoBite: One working order: Sun Physics, Mon Maths, Tue Hindi, Wed English, Thu Biology, Fri off, Sat Chemistry. The off day must come just before Chemistry.

question:
A passage consists of 6 sentences. The first and sixth sentences of the passage are at their correct positions, while the middle four sentences (represented by P, Q, R, and S) are jumbled up.
First sentence: Smoke oozed up between the planks.
P: Passengers were told to be ready to quit the ship.
Q: The rising gale fanned the smouldering fire.
R: Everyone now knew there was fire onboard.
S: Flames broke out here and there.
Sixth sentence: Most people bore the shock bravely.
The most logically CORRECT order for the given jumbled up sentences is
infoBite: Smoke → the gale fans the fire (Q) → flames break out (S) → everyone knows (R) → passengers told to be ready (P) → they bear the shock.

question:
For a painting to succeed, it is essential that the painter and his public agree about what is significant. The subject of the painting may have a personal meaning for the painter or a common person; but there can also be the possibility of their agreement on its general meaning. It is at this point that the culture of the society and the period in question precedes the artists and her/his art. Renaissance art would have meant nothing to the Aztecs, and vice versa. If, to some extent, a few intellectuals can appreciate them both today, it is because their culture is a historical one. Its inspiration is history and all known developments to date.
According to the passage, which of the following is/are NOT necessarily among the attributes needed for a painter to succeed?

options.A: The subject must have a personal meaning for the painter.
options.B: The painter is able to communicate and justify the significance of its subject selection.
options.C: The painter and the public agree on what is significant.
options.D: The painting of the subjects is driven by public demand.

infoBite: The passage says only agreement on significance is essential; personal meaning is merely possible (“may”), and public demand is never required.
note: The official key accepts A OR D. The app takes one answer, so A is stored; D is also marked correct in the real exam.

question:
Vinod has a pre-determined route. Each morning he delivers 37 newspapers to customers in his neighborhood. It takes Vinod 50 minutes to deliver all the papers. When Vinod was sick or had other engagements, his friend Tarun, who lives on the same street delivered the papers on his behalf.
Find the statement(s) that must be TRUE according to the given information.

options.A: Vinod and Tarun lived in the same locality.
options.B: It was dark outside when Vinod began his delivery.
options.C: It took Tarun more than 50 minutes to deliver the papers.

infoBite: Tarun lives on the same street and covers the same fixed route, so A and D must be true. Darkness and Tarun's speed are never mentioned.

question:
Cholera, typhoid, diphtheria and tuberculosis cause huge number of deaths. Poor quality drinking water has always been the world’s greatest single carrier of sickness. Disease is transmitted when sewage and drinking water come into contact. Children are particularly vulnerable. In some of the poorest countries the infant mortality rate is high. The separation of sewage and the supply of clean drinking water are the domain of civil engineers, and their work makes a significant contribution to public health. That contribution was recognized when public sanitation was voted the greatest medical breakthrough, beating the discoveries including antibiotics and vaccines in a poll organized by the British Medical Journal.
Identify the statement(s), which is/are NOT TRUE according to the passage.

options.A: Children are less prone to water borne diseases.
options.B: The infant mortality rate was high in economically weaker countries.
options.C: The provision of sewage and drinking water should be adequately separated from each other.
options.D: The literature states that the public health and sanitation was never given its due importance.

infoBite: Children are said to be “particularly vulnerable”, and sanitation was voted the greatest medical breakthrough, so A and D contradict the passage.
note: The official key accepts A;D OR A;B;D (B says “was high in economically weaker countries”, while the passage says “some of the poorest”). The app stores A;D.

question:
Shark’s teeth have evolved to correspond to the diet of each particular species of shark. Consequently, the teeth of the great white shark bear little resemblance to those of the bull shark or nurse shark. There were essentially four different shark diets and thus four varieties of shark teeth. Sharks that feed on fish have needle like teeth, perfect for spearing and ripping. Sharks that eat mammals such as seals and sea lions have heavy, serrated teeth, typically triangular on the upper jaw and pointed on the lower jaw. Shark that feed in the benthic zone of the ocean have flattened teeth for crushing the shell of the creatures they find scuttling in the sand or clinging to rocks. Sharks that bask have teeth that are largely non-functional; these sharks filter food from the water by passing it through their gills.
Which of the following is/are the CORRECT inference(s) as per the passage?

options.A: Shark’s teeth are not specially designed for slaughter.
options.B: The shape of the shark’s teeth relates to its prey.
options.C: Some species of sharks filter food through their gills.
options.D: Shark’s teeth relate to its diet.

infoBite: Each tooth type matches a diet (needle, serrated, flattened, non-functional), and basking sharks filter food through their gills.

question:
A particular school management wants to contact all parents, all businessmen and all engineers. The following statistics are available with the school.
Businessmen = 50
Engineers = 25
Parents = 2500
Businessmen who are engineers = 0
Businessmen who are parents = 25
Engineers who are parents = 15
The number of people needs to be contacted are _______ .
infoBite: Union = 50 + 25 + 2500 − 0 − 25 − 15 + 0 = 2535 (no one is in all three groups, since no businessman is an engineer).
note: Official key: 2535 to 2535.

question:
“He who is unable to live in society, or who has no need because he is sufficient for himself, must be either a beast or a god.”
Who has given the above statement?
infoBite: From Aristotle's Politics, Book I, where he calls man “by nature a political animal” (zōon politikon) whose life is fulfilled in the polis.

question:
“History is not made only in statecraft; its lasting results are produced in the ranks of learned men.”
Name the play from which the above excerpt has been taken.

options.A: Mahesh Dattani’s Thirty Days in September
options.B: Vijay Tendulkar’s Silence! The Court is in Session

works: Silence! The Court Is in Session
infoBite: Tughlaq (Kannada 1964; Karnad's English version 1971) shows the idealist sultan Muhammad bin Tughlaq; the historian Barani is the scholar he confides in. Karnad also appears in GATE 2023 (Hayavadana) and 2026 (play list).
note: Answer follows the key; the line's exact place in the play couldn't be confirmed independently.

question: Who amongst the following popularised the term ‘objective correlative’, which is often used in formalist criticism?
infoBite: Eliot used it in “Hamlet and His Problems” (1919): a set of objects, a situation or chain of events that evokes a particular emotion. The American painter Washington Allston had used the phrase earlier.

question: Which of the following critics preferred Shakespeare’s comedies to his tragedies?
infoBite: In the Preface to Shakespeare (1765) Johnson writes that Shakespeare's tragedy seems to be skill, his comedy instinct. Shakespeare criticism was also asked in GATE 2025 (Dryden, Lamb, Coleridge, Arnold).

question: Who among the following has been credited with laying the foundation of comparative literature by Russian Formalists?
infoBite: Veselovsky's comparative “historical poetics” (19th century) was the starting point the Formalists argued with. Shklovsky gave “defamiliarisation”, Propp the 31 functions of the folktale, Jakobson the six functions of language.

question: Lyrical Ballads, considered to be the manifesto of Romantic Poetry, was first published in the year ________.
infoBite: Lyrical Ballads appeared anonymously in 1798, opening with Coleridge's “The Rime of the Ancient Mariner” and closing with “Tintern Abbey”. Wordsworth's Preface came in the 1800 edition and was expanded in 1802.

question:
Identify the work from which the following excerpt has been taken:
“In a universe that is suddenly deprived of illusions and of light, man feels a stranger. He is an irremediable exile …. This divorce between man and his life, the actor and his setting, truly constitutes the feeling of Absurdity.”

options.C: Albert Camus’ The Myth of Sisyphus

infoBite: Camus's essay The Myth of Sisyphus (1942) ends by imagining Sisyphus happy. Martin Esslin's “Theatre of the Absurd” (asked GATE 2023) borrows Camus's idea for Beckett and Pinter.

question: What does gynocriticism recommend as an approach to literature?

options.A: Considering women’s literature from men’s point of view
options.B: Examining women’s literature confirming gender stereotypes only
options.C: Becoming more familiar with the history of women and women’s writing

infoBite: Showalter coined “gynocritics” in “Towards a Feminist Poetics” (1979): the study of women as writers and of a female literary tradition. Her A Literature of Their Own was asked in GATE 2025. Gerontology is the study of ageing.

question:
Identify the novel which opens with the following lines:
“It was the best of times, it was the worst of times, it was the age of wisdom, it was the age of foolishness, it was the epoch of belief, it was the epoch of incredulity, it was the season of light, it was the season of darkness, it was the spring of hope, it was the winter of despair.”

options.C: Charles Dickens’ A Tale of Two Cities
options.D: H. G. Wells’ The Time Machine

infoBite: The antithesis-filled opening of A Tale of Two Cities (1859), set in London and Paris around the French Revolution. Asked again in GATE 2026; opening lines also came up in GATE 2023 (Pride and Prejudice).

question: Which of the following terms does not form a part of seven types of ambiguities propounded by William Empson?
infoBite: Empson, a pupil of I. A. Richards, published Seven Types of Ambiguity in 1930; his examples involve metaphor, simile and pun. “Simulacra” is Baudrillard's term (asked GATE 2023 and in Q62 here).

question: Which of the following poem(s) has/have been influenced by Hindu philosophy?
infoBite: Emerson's “Brahma” (1857) echoes the Bhagavad Gita and Katha Upanishad (“If the red slayer think he slays…”). Southey's The Curse of Kehama (1810) is an epic built on Hindu myth. “Kubla Khan” is about the Mongol emperor.

question: Which of the following human behaviour(s) is/are important to a Freudian psychoanalytical study of William Shakespeare’s Hamlet?
infoBite: Freud linked Hamlet's delay to the Oedipus complex in The Interpretation of Dreams (1900); Ernest Jones expanded it in Hamlet and Oedipus (1949).

question: Which of the following novel-author combination(s) is/are correct?

options.A: Where Shall We Go This Summer – Jane Austen
options.B: A Passage to England – Nirad C Chaudhuri
options.C: The Mayor of Casterbridge – Thomas Hardy

works: Where Shall We Go This Summer?
infoBite: Where Shall We Go This Summer? (1975) is Anita Desai's; Pride and Prejudice (1813) is Austen's — the options swap them. The Mayor of Casterbridge appeared in 1886; Chaudhuri also wrote The Autobiography of an Unknown Indian (1951).
note: A Passage to England (1959) is a travel book rather than a novel; the official key still counts B as a correct pairing.

question: Which of the following statements is/are correct about Phenomenology?

options.A: It is a form of methodological idealism, seeking to explore an abstraction called ‘human consciousness’.
options.B: It is a philosophical method associated with Edmund Husserl.
options.C: It believes that the act of thinking and the object of thought are internally related, mutually dependent.
options.D: Heidegger’s Being and Time is an important phenomenological treatise supporting the stand of Husserl.

infoBite: Husserl's phenomenology brackets the external world to study consciousness, where act and object of thought are bound together. Heidegger's Being and Time (1927) broke with his teacher, so D is wrong. It later fed the Geneva School and reader-response theory.

question: Chitra Divakaruni’s The Mistress of Spices is ________.
infoBite: The Mistress of Spices (1997) follows Tilo, who runs an Indian spice shop in Oakland and uses magical spices to help immigrant customers. Magic realism was also asked in GATE 2023 and 2024.

question: Which of the following is/are correct about postmodernist critics?

options.A: They foreground fiction and exemplify ‘disappearance of the real’.
options.D: They challenge the distinction between high and low cultures.

infoBite: Postmodernism blurs high and low culture (Jameson), plays with irony (Hutcheon) and treats the real as lost in simulation (Baudrillard).
note: The official key leaves out C (reflexivity), though self-reflexivity is often listed as postmodern; the key's answer A;B;D is used.

question: The literary theory of Deconstruction argues that ________.

options.B: the meaning of a text never relies on context
options.C: any system for the production of meaning may be bound by context, yet also limitless
options.D: texts are always rigid in meaning

infoBite: For Derrida meaning is context-bound but context is never fully saturated, so meaning is always open (“Signature Event Context”, 1972). Deconstruction was also asked in GATE 2023 (Yale School, Spivak).

question: In the context of the Reader-Response Theory, Louise M Rosenblatt in her essay “The Poem as Event”, considers that the reader should ________.

options.A: participate in a transaction with the text
options.C: be acted upon by the text

works: The Reader, the Text, the Poem
infoBite: Rosenblatt's transactional theory treats the poem as an event between reader and text, developed in The Reader, the Text, the Poem (1978). Reader-response was asked again in GATE 2025 (Stanley Fish).
note: The official key also counts C (“be acted upon by the text”), as part of the two-way transaction.

question: Roland Barthes in his famous essay, “The Death of the Author” ________.

options.A: believes that the text is to be interpreted in the biographical context of the author
options.B: challenges the author’s claim as “cogito”, or origin of all knowledge
options.C: believes that the author has sole claim to his work
options.D: concludes that an author is an atypical product of his social milieu

infoBite: Barthes's essay (1967 in English, 1968 in French) ends: the birth of the reader must be at the cost of the death of the Author. Meaning comes from language and the reader, not the author's biography.
note: The official C2 key couldn't be opened for this question. B follows Collegedunia's worked solution and is the only option consistent with the essay.

question:
What is common among the following novels?
Cormac McCarthy’s The Road
George Orwell’s Nineteen Eighty Four
Margaret Atwood’s The Handmaid’s Tale

options.A: These are examples of Utopian fiction.
options.B: These are examples of Dystopian fiction.
options.C: They present an idealistic picture of the world.
options.D: They abound in pleasant descriptions of landscapes, peoples and places.

infoBite: The Road (2006, Pulitzer 2007) is post-apocalyptic; Nineteen Eighty-Four (1949) and The Handmaid's Tale (1985) are totalitarian dystopias. Both Orwell and Atwood dystopias were asked again in GATE 2026.

question:
Match the following authors with their pseudonyms:
i. George Eliot
ii. Sylvia Plath
iii. H. H. Munro
iv. Charlotte Brontë

a. Victoria Lucas
b. Currer Bell
c. Mary Ann Evans
d. Saki
infoBite: Mary Ann Evans wrote as George Eliot; Plath published The Bell Jar as Victoria Lucas (asked GATE 2023); H. H. Munro wrote as Saki; Charlotte Brontë was Currer Bell. Pseudonyms recur: GATE 2023 and 2024 (Orwell) too.

question:
“This literary mode parallels the flouting of authority and inversion of social hierarchies that, in many cultures, are permitted in a season of …. It does so by introducing a mingling of voices from diverse social levels that are free to mock and subvert authority, to flout social norms by ribaldry, and to exhibit various ways of profaning what is ordinarily regarded as sacrosanct.”
The above description explains the concept of ________.
infoBite: The passage is close to Abrams's Glossary entry on Bakhtin's carnivalesque (Rabelais and His World, 1965). Heteroglossia, also Bakhtin's, means the many voices within a novel's language.

question:
“Postcolonial perspectives emerge from the colonial testimony of Third World countries and the discourses of ‘minorities’ within the geopolitical divisions of East and West, North and South. They intervene in those ideological discourses of modernity that attempt to give a hegemonic ‘normality’ to the uneven development and the differential, often disadvantaged, histories of nations, races, communities, people.”
The above commentary on the postcolonial perspective has been extracted from which of the following?

options.B: Homi K Bhabha’s The Location of Culture
options.D: Bill Ashcroft et al., eds. The Post-colonial Studies Reader

infoBite: From the chapter “The postcolonial and the postmodern” in Bhabha's The Location of Culture (1994), the book of hybridity, mimicry and the “third space”. Orientalism appeared in 1978.

question:
Match the following excerpts with their authors:
i. Rapt, twirling in thy hand a withered spray, / And waiting for the spark from heaven to fall.
ii. Shakespeare one gets acquainted with without knowing how. It is part of an English man’s constitution. His thoughts and beauties are so spread abroad that one touches upon them everywhere, one is intimate with him by instinct.
iii. It is as natural to die as to be born; and to a little infant, perhaps, the one is as painful as the other.
iv. Happiness was but the occasional episode in a general drama of pain.

a. Jane Austen
b. Thomas Hardy
c. Matthew Arnold
d. Francis Bacon
infoBite: i: Arnold's “The Scholar-Gipsy” (1853). ii: Henry Crawford in Austen's Mansfield Park (1814). iii: Bacon's essay “Of Death”. iv: the last sentence of Hardy's The Mayor of Casterbridge (1886).

question: Which of the following statements is the most appropriate in the context of Francoise d’ Eaubonne’s concept of Eco-feminism?

options.A: It is a revolution by women against men to protect Nature.
options.B: It is a philosophical idea to counter the oppression of women by men, as similar to the oppression and destruction of Nature by men.
options.C: It is a term used to describe how the human race could be saved by men initiating an ecological revolution.
options.D: It is a term used to describe the interface between women and technology.

infoBite: D'Eaubonne coined “écoféminisme” in Le Féminisme ou la mort (1974), linking patriarchal domination of women with domination of nature. Ecocriticism was asked in GATE 2023.
