question: Which of the following books is considered as one of the sources behind T. S. Eliot’s poem, The Waste Land?

options.B: Jessie Weston’s From Ritual to Romance

infoBite: Eliot's notes to The Waste Land (1922) name Jessie Weston's From Ritual to Romance (1920, the Grail and Fisher King) and Frazer's The Golden Bough (an option in GATE 2023).

question:
“The people who believe most that our greatness and welfare are proved by our being very rich, and who most give their lives and thoughts to becoming rich, are just the very people whom we call Philistines.”
What can be inferred from the above statement of Matthew Arnold?

options.A: Greatness of people lies in their being rich and prosperous.
options.B: Material prosperity is not the true criterion of a nation’s achievement.
options.D: Arnold thinks very highly of himself.

infoBite: From “Sweetness and Light” in Culture and Anarchy (1869), where Arnold sorts English society into Barbarians (aristocracy), Philistines (middle class) and Populace.

question: ‘Anagnorisis’, as used by Aristotle in his theory of Tragedy, stands for ________.

options.A: the hero’s recognition of his tragic flaw
options.B: the hero’s ignorance about his tragic flaw
options.C: the hero’s recognition of his adversary
options.D: the hero’s rejection of his tragic end

infoBite: In the Poetics anagnorisis is a change from ignorance to knowledge, ideally together with peripeteia (reversal), as when Oedipus learns who he is. Hubris and hamartia were asked in GATE 2023.

question: Which of the following thinkers does not belong to the school of Existentialism?
infoBite: Kierkegaard is called the father of existentialism; Sartre (Being and Nothingness, 1943) defined it as “existence precedes essence”. Barthes was a structuralist and post-structuralist (Q45).

question: Which of the following statement(s) is/are closely associated with the term Fetishism?

options.A: It is generally defined as an act of paying excessive attention or attributing mystical ability, to an inanimate thing.
options.B: It is related to Western theories of aesthetics, economics and psychology.
options.C: It is used in reference to religious objects believed to have magical or spiritual powers.
options.D: It is generally used to describe Gothic expressionism.

infoBite: The word comes from Portuguese feitiço (charm). Marx gave “commodity fetishism” (Capital, 1867) and Freud wrote “Fetishism” (1927).

question:
Why does the thin grey strand
Floating up from the forgotten
Cigarette between my fingers,
Why does it trouble me?
Ah, you will understand;
When I carried my mother downstairs,
A few times only, at the beginning
Of her soft-foot malady,
I should find, for a reprimand
To my gaiety, a few long grey hairs
On the breast of my coat; and one by one
I watched them float up the dark chimney.
Which of the following can be considered as correct about the above poem?

options.A: It is written in the process of grieving for the poet’s mother.
options.D: It is a poem of youthful celebration.

infoBite: This is D. H. Lawrence's “Sorrow”, one of his poems on his mother's illness and death in 1910; the rising smoke recalls her grey hairs drifting up the chimney.

question: Which of the given examples of rhetorical/figurative devices is/are correctly paired?

options.A: ‘What is man, that thou art mindful of him?’ : Paradox
options.C: ‘Reading furnishes the mind only with material of knowledge; it is thinking makes what we read ours.’ : Antithesis
options.D: ‘It is a truth universally acknowledged that a single man in possession of a good fortune must be in want of a wife.’ : Irony

works: Of the Conduct of the Understanding
infoBite: A is a rhetorical question (Psalm 8) and B a paradox. C sets reading against thinking (Locke); D is the ironic opening of Pride and Prejudice, asked directly in GATE 2023.

question: As per the distinctions made by Toril Moi, regarding the terms ‘feminist’, ‘female’ and ‘feminine’, which of the following is/are correct?

options.A: The first is ‘a matter of economic manumission’.
options.B: The second is a ‘matter of psychology’.
options.D: The third is a set of ‘culturally defined characteristics’.

infoBite: In “Feminist, Female, Feminine” (1989) Moi separates feminist (a political position), female (a matter of biology) and feminine (culturally defined traits). She also wrote Sexual/Textual Politics (1985).

question: Which of the following author(s) has/have won the Booker Prize twice?
works: True History of the Kelly Gang
infoBite: Farrell won in 1973 (The Siege of Krishnapur) and the 2010 “Lost Man Booker” (Troubles); Carey in 1988 and 2001. Coetzee, Mantel and Atwood have also won twice. Booker questions recur: GATE 2025 and 2026.

question:
“Nothing feels normal to Ashima, it’s not so much the pain which she will survive. Its consequence: motherhood in a foreign land … unmonitored by those she loves … she is terrified to raise a child in a country where she knows so little, where life seems so tentative and spare.”
In the above passage of The Namesake, the writer tries to say that Ashima ________.

options.A: feels isolated in the new world
options.B: should have been surrounded by her own people
options.D: is able to adapt herself to an alien culture

infoBite: Ashima Ganguli gives birth to Gogol in Cambridge, Massachusetts, far from her family in Calcutta. Lahiri's The Namesake (2003) followed her Pulitzer-winning Interpreter of Maladies (1999).

question: Jean Baudrillard, a post-modern thinker, has suggested that a sign refers to other signs. He has given four stages/phases to support his proposition. Which of the following do(es) not constitute a part of these stages/phases?

options.A: The sign disguises the fact that there is no corresponding reality underneath.
options.C: The sign bears no relation to any reality at all.
options.D: The sign misrepresents or distorts the reality behind it.

infoBite: Baudrillard's four phases (Simulacra and Simulation, 1981): the image reflects reality, masks and distorts it, masks its absence, then has no relation to any reality — the pure simulacrum. Simulacra was asked in GATE 2023.
note: MSQ in the paper with a single correct option in the key.

question: Which of the following apply/applies to the term ‘parapraxis’?

options.A: It is used in connection with Marxist interpretation of literature.
options.B: It refers to an error in speech, memory, or physical action that occurs because of the interference of an unconscious subdued wish.
options.C: The term is generally associated with Jung.
options.D: The original German word referring to the term is ‘Fehlleistung’.

infoBite: Parapraxis, the “Freudian slip”, is the translators' word for Freud's Fehlleistung (“faulty action”), discussed in The Psychopathology of Everyday Life (1901). It is Freud's term, not Jung's.

question:
The epilogue to William Congreve’s The Way of the World, given below, signals some warning(s). What is/are it/they?
“Other there are whose malice we’d prevent,
Such, who watch plays, with scurrilous intent
To mark out who by characters are meant.
These, with false glosses feed their own ill nature,
And turn to libel, what was meant a satire.”

options.A: Critics should always be supportive of the author.
options.B: Critics should not look for portrait of real people in the play’s characters and remember that the play is a social satire.
options.C: Critics should avoid writing malicious reviews, lest they are accused of libel.
options.D: Critics should try to identify the real life equivalent for each character.

infoBite: The Way of the World (1700), with Mirabell and Millamant, is the peak of Restoration comedy of manners. It was also an option in GATE 2025 (works not by Dryden).

question:
Read the following lines and mark your correct observation(s):
Take my shirt off
and go in there to do the puja
No thanks.
Not me.
But you go right ahead
if that’s what you want to do.
Give me the match box
before you go,
will you?
I will be out in the courtyard
where no one will mind it
if I smoke.

options.A: The poem is written in the form of an ode.
options.B: The poem is skeptic in nature.
options.C: The poet uses surreal and astonishing images.
options.D: The poem expresses a rebellious attitude.

infoBite: The lines are from Arun Kolatkar's Jejuri (1976; Commonwealth Poetry Prize 1977), a sequence of 31 poems about a secular visitor to the temple town. The speaker politely declines the puja and smokes outside.

question:
Consider the following sentences:
(i) After his surgery, Raja hardly could walk.
(ii) After his surgery, Raja could barely walk.
(iii) After his surgery, Raja barely could walk.
(iv) After his surgery, Raja could hardly walk.
Which of the above sentences are grammatically CORRECT?
infoBite: Adverbs like “hardly” and “barely” go after the modal verb: “could hardly walk”, “could barely walk”.

question: Ms. X came out of a building through its front door to find her shadow due to the morning sun falling to her right side with the building to her back. From this, it can be inferred that building is facing _________
infoBite: The morning sun is in the east, so her shadow points west. West on her right means she faces south — the same way as the building's front door.

question:
In the figure, O is the center of the circle and, M and N lie on the circle.
The area of the right triangle MON is 50 cm².
What is the area of the circle in cm²?
infoBite: OM and ON are both radii and form the right angle, so r²/2 = 50, giving r² = 100 and an area of 100π.
note: The original has a simple figure (right angle at O); the text is enough to solve it.

question: If “⊕” means “−”, “⊗” means “÷”, “△” means “+” and “∇” means “×”, then the value of the expression 2 ⊕ 3 △ ((4 ⊗ 2) ∇ 4) =
note: The operator symbols are images in the official PDF; they are written here with ⊕ ⊗ △ ∇.

question:
“The increased consumption of leafy vegetables in the recent months is a clear indication that the people in the state have begun to lead a healthy lifestyle”
Which of the following can be logically inferred from the information presented in the above statement?

options.A: The people in the state did not consume leafy vegetables earlier.
options.B: Consumption of leafy vegetables may not be the only indicator of healthy lifestyle.
options.C: Leading a healthy lifestyle is related to a diet with leafy vegetables.
options.D: The people in the state have increased awareness of health hazards causing by consumption of junk foods.

infoBite: The claim only works if eating leafy vegetables is linked to a healthy lifestyle. It says consumption increased, not that it was zero before, so A goes too far.

question:
Oxpeckers and rhinos manifest a symbiotic relationship in the wild. The oxpeckers warn the rhinos about approaching poachers, thus possibly saving the lives of the rhinos. Oxpeckers also feed on the parasitic ticks found on rhinos.
In the symbiotic relationship described above, the primary benefits for oxpeckers and rhinos respectively are,

options.A: Oxpeckers get a food source, rhinos have no benefit.
options.B: Oxpeckers save their habitat from poachers while the rhinos have no benefit.
options.C: Oxpeckers get a food source, rhinos may be saved from the poachers.
options.D: Oxpeckers save the lives of poachers, rhinos save their own lives.

infoBite: Each side gains: the birds eat ticks, and their warnings may save the rhinos. “May” matches the passage's “possibly”.

question:
The number of hens, ducks and goats in farm P are 65, 91 and 169, respectively. The total number of hens, ducks and goats in a nearby farm Q is 416. The ratio of hens:ducks:goats in farm Q is 5:14:13. All the hens, ducks and goats are sent from farm Q to farm P.
The new ratio of hens:ducks:goats in farm P is_____
infoBite: Farm Q: 416 ÷ 32 = 13, so 65 hens, 182 ducks, 169 goats. Farm P then has 130 : 273 : 338 = 10 : 21 : 26.

question:
Five persons P, Q, R, S and T are sitting in a row not necessarily in the same order. Q and R are separated by one person, and S should not be seated adjacent to Q.
The number of distinct seating arrangements possible is:
infoBite: Q and R with one seat between them can sit 6 ways. Counting where S may go each time gives 4 + 2 + 2 + 2 + 2 + 4 = 16.

question:
According to a recent article in a medical journal, consuming curcumin (from turmeric) significantly lowers the risk of COVID-19. The researchers draw this conclusion from a study that found that people who consumed one or more teaspoons of curcumin extract everyday were half as likely to be diagnosed with the disease as people who did not consume curcumin.
Which of the following, if true, most weakens the argument in the article?

options.A: In another study, people who were given a zinc supplement everyday were more than four times less likely to be diagnosed with COVID-19 as those who did not.
options.B: All the participants in this study were from the same state where no other spices or herbs are consumed.
options.C: The participants who consumed curcumin were also more likely to exercise than those who did not.
options.D: In another study, COVID-19 patients who were given curcumin were no more likely to recover than others.

infoBite: Exercise is another possible cause of the lower risk, so curcumin may not be the reason. D is about recovery, not about getting the disease.

question:
Froot Inc. carried out an internet advertisement campaign for its new beverage CocoLoco. After the campaign, the director of the advertising company conducted a survey and found that the CocoLoco sales were higher than that of TenderJoos a competing product from Joos Inc. The agency concluded that the internet advertising campaign is more effective than advertising through other media.
Which of the following statements could strengthen the conclusion above by the agency?

options.A: A ₹2 discount was offered on CocoLoco during the campaign period.
options.B: CocoLoco sales were higher than those of TenderJoos before the internet campaign.
options.C: A newspaper advertisement campaign the previous year did not increase CocoLoco sales.
options.D: During the campaign for CocoLoco, Joos Inc. did not advertise TenderJoos at all.

infoBite: The claim compares internet ads with other media, so evidence that newspaper ads failed supports it. A, B and D give other reasons for the higher sales.

question:
An e-commerce site offered a deal last month conditional on the customer spending a minimum of ₹500. Any customer who buys 2 kg of fresh fruit will receive a hand mixer and any customer who buys 2 kg of fresh vegetables will receive a vegetable chopper.
Which of the following is NOT a possible outcome of the above?

options.A: A customer purchased 3 kg of fresh fruit and did not receive a vegetable chopper.
options.B: A customer purchased items for ₹500 which included 1 kg of vegetables and received a hand mixer.
options.C: A customer purchased items for ₹500 which included 2 kg of vegetables and 1 kg of fruit and received a hand mixer.
options.D: A customer purchased items for ₹300 which included 2 kg of fruit and received neither a hand mixer nor a vegetable chopper.

infoBite: With only 1 kg of fruit, C's order can't earn the hand mixer. B's other items could include 2 kg of fruit, and D is below the ₹500 minimum.

question:
Writers of detective fiction often include an incompetent detective as a foil for the brilliant investigator-protagonist as they follow different paths in trying to solve the crime. In the individual accounts, the incompetent detective is frequently distracted by the culprit’s careful plans, while the competent investigator solves the case after a final confrontation. Analysts of such fiction believe that the authors select this story-telling technique to provide readers with more complexities in the form of misleading clues, while figuring out the crime.
Which of the following statements most logically follows from the passage above?

options.A: A detective story is considered well-written if the brilliant investigator is accompanied by an incompetent detective.
options.B: Writers of detective fiction use the contrast of an incompetent detective to mainly show how complex the investigation is.
options.C: Writers of detective fiction never write stories where the incompetent detective solves the case.
options.D: Writers of detective fiction use two investigative accounts to make it difficult for the reader to figure out the outcome.

infoBite: The passage says the two paths give readers misleading clues, which makes the outcome harder to guess. Think of Inspector Lestrade beside Sherlock Holmes.

question:
The first (P1) and the last (P6) parts of a single sentence are given to you. The rest of the sentence is divided into four parts and labelled (L,M,N,O). Reorder these parts so that the sentence can be read through correctly and select one of the options given.
P1: Studies of several Sahitya Akademi award winners show that…
L: or encounter professional
M: and invariably develop a strained relationship with other literary figures
N: they often publish very little
O: after winning the prize
P6: …envy and rivalry.
The correct order is:
infoBite: “…show that after winning the prize they often publish very little and invariably develop a strained relationship with other literary figures or encounter professional envy and rivalry.”

question:
Gerrymandering refers to the targeted redrawing of election constituencies so as to benefit a particular party. This is especially important where the electoral system is “first past the post” in each constituency (i.e. one winner is selected in each constituency based on a majority of votes won) and where there is no other provision for proportional representation (as for example in the German system). For a simple illustration of gerrymandering, if a region consists of districts 1, 2, 3, …, 9 with districts 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 favouring party P and 7, 8, 9 favouring party Q, then grouping of districts to constituencies as {1,2,3}, {4,5,6}, {7,8,9} will give two seats to party P and one seat to party Q, whereas the grouping {1,2,7}, {3,4,8}, {5,6,9} will give all three seats to party P, as they will secure a majority in each constituency.
Which of these statements can be deduced from the above?

options.A: Gerrymandering implies that constituency boundaries can sometimes be drawn to favour one party over the other.
options.B: Gerrymandering implies that proportional representation is impossible when districts are grouped to form constituencies.
options.C: To counteract gerrymandering political parties should concentrate on districts where they are favoured.
options.D: The grouping of districts to constituencies has very little impact on proportional representation.

infoBite: The example shows the same votes giving 2–1 or 3–0 depending only on how districts are grouped. B overstates it; D contradicts the example.

question:
X-ray examination of a recently discovered painting that some authorities judge to be a self-portrait by Michelangelo revealed an under-image of a woman’s face. Either Michelangelo or some other artist must have repainted over the first painting that had now been seen on the canvas. Because the woman’s face also appears on other paintings by Michelangelo, this painting is determined to indeed be an authentic painting by Michelangelo.
Which of the following assumptions must be made in reaching the conclusion above?

options.A: When an already painted canvas of an artist is used, the second artist using that canvas for a new painting is usually influenced by the artistic style of the first.
options.B: Several painted canvases that art historians attribute to Michelangelo contain under-images that appear on at least one other of Michelangelo’s paintings.
options.C: Subject or subjects that appear in authenticated paintings of Michelangelo are rather unlikely to show up as under-images on painted canvases not attributed to Michelangelo.
options.D: No painted canvas can be attributed to a particular artist with certainty without an X-ray analysis.

infoBite: The face proves authorship only if other artists are unlikely to have painted it too. Without that assumption, another painter could have reused the canvas.

question:
This season _______ tourists visited Ladakh than last season; however, ______ to be the biggest tourist destination in India. The tourism department explains that the number of tourists to India has ______ relative to previous years, ________ have chosen to visit Ladakh.
Select the correct sequence of phrases to fill in the blanks to complete the passage above.

options.A: more / for the first time in many seasons it does not appear / increased / and it seems that most
options.B: fewer / as in the past, it appears / in fact decreased / but it seems that only a small proportion
options.C: fewer / for the first time in many seasons it appears / in fact decreased / but it seems that most
options.D: more / this season as well, it appears / in fact decreased / but it seems that a large proportion

infoBite: “However” needs a contrast: fewer tourists, yet Ladakh is the top destination, because India's total fell but most visitors chose Ladakh.

question:
Reorder the sentences in (1) – (5) such that they form a coherent paragraph.
(1) In fact, dozens of languages today have only one native speaker still living, and that person's death will mean the extinction of the language: It will no longer be spoken, or known, by anyone on earth.
(2) Many languages are falling out of use and are being replaced by others that are more widely used in the region or nation, such as English in Australia or Portuguese in Brazil.
(3) Many other languages are no longer being learned by new generations of children or by new adult speakers.
(4) An endangered language is one that is likely to become extinct in the near future.
(5) Unless the trends are reversed, these endangered languages will become extinct by the end of the century.
(Adapted from What is an Endangered Language by A. Woodbury.)
infoBite: Definition first (4), then two causes (2, 3), the extreme case introduced by “In fact” (1), and the warning “Unless the trends are reversed” (5).

question:
The first (P1) and the last (P6) parts of a single sentence are given to you. The rest of the sentence is divided into four parts and labelled L,M,N,O. Reorder these parts so that the sentence can be read correctly and select one of the sequences below.
P1: For a little while…
L: it was a common belief
M: right after the treaty of Versailles
N: that Germany had caused World War I not just by her actions
O: held by analysts and politicians alike
P6: … but by also encouraging Italy in her own aggressions.
infoBite: “For a little while right after the treaty of Versailles it was a common belief held by analysts and politicians alike that Germany had caused World War I not just by her actions but…” The treaty was signed in June 1919.

question:
After Florentino Ariza saw her for the first time, his mother knew before he told her because he lost his voice and his appetite and spent the entire night tossing and turning in his bed. But when he began to wait for the answer to his first letter, his anguish was complicated by diaorrhea and green vomit, he became disoriented and suffered from sudden fainting spells, and his mother was terrified because his condition did not resemble the turmoil of love so much as the devastation of cholera. Florentino Ariza’s godfather, an old homeopathic practitioner who had been Tránsito Ariza’s confidant ever since her days as a secret mistress, was also alarmed at first by the patient’s condition, because he had the weak pulse, the hoarse breathing, and the pale perspiration of a dying man. But his examination revealed that he had no fever, no pain anywhere, and that his only concrete feeling was an urgent desire to die. All that was needed was shrewd questioning, first of the patient and then of his mother, to conclude once again that the symptoms of love were the same as those of cholera. He prescribed infusions of linden blossoms to calm the nerves and suggested a change of air so he could find consolation in distance, but Florentino Ariza longed for just the opposite: to enjoy his martyrdom.
(Adapted from Love in a Time of Cholera by Gabriel García Márquez.)
The author of the passage is implying that:

options.B: The doctor could not distinguish between love and cholera.
options.C: The doctor could distinguish between love and cholera.
options.D: The symptoms of love and cholera are similar.

works: Love in the Time of Cholera
infoBite: The godfather sees through the symptoms by questioning, so he can tell love from cholera. Love in the Time of Cholera (1985) follows Florentino Ariza's lifelong love for Fermina Daza.

question:
Now, it is clear that the decline of a language must ultimately have political and economic causes: it is not due simply to the bad influence of this or that individual writer. But an effect can become a cause, reinforcing the original cause and producing the same effect in an intensified form, and so on indefinitely. A man may take to drink because he feels himself to be a failure, and then fail all the more completely because he drinks. It is rather the same thing that is happening to the English language. It becomes ugly and inaccurate because our thoughts are foolish, but the slovenliness of our language makes it easier for us to have foolish thoughts.
(Adapted from Politics and the English Language by George Orwell.)
The illustration of the man who takes to drink is used to underscore which of the following ideas in the passage above?

options.A: Political and economic causes control deterioration of language.
options.B: Foolish thoughts are enabled by inaccurate language.
options.C: Effect of an action becomes the cause in a cyclic pattern.
options.D: Drinking enables people to have foolish thoughts and slovenly language.

infoBite: Orwell's essay (1946) ends with six rules for clear writing. The drinker shows a vicious circle: bad thinking spoils language, and spoilt language feeds bad thinking.

question:
It is a pity that Caste even today has its defenders. The defences are many. It is defended on the grounds that the Caste System is but another name for division of labour, and if division of labour is a necessary feature of every civilised society, then it is argued that there is nothing wrong in the Caste System. Now the first thing to be urged against this view is that Caste System is not merely division of labour. It is also a division of labourers. Civilised society undoubtedly needs division of labour but nowhere is division of labour accompanied by this unnatural division of labourers into watertight compartments, grading them one above the other. This division of labour is not spontaneous or based on natural aptitudes. Social and individual efficiency requires us to develop the individual capacity and competency to choose and to make his own career. This principle is violated in so far as it involves an attempt to appoint tasks to individuals in advance, not on the basis of trained original capacities, but on that of birth. Industry undergoes rapid and abrupt changes and an individual must be free to change his occupation and adjust himself to changing circumstances, to gain his livelihood. (Adapted from Annihilation of Caste by Dr. B.R. Ambedkar.)
Which of the following observations substantiate the arguments found in the passage above?

options.A: Newer generations are unable to change and move away from low-paying family professions, even with changed economic circumstances.
options.B: Sedentary desk jobs are considered to have more value and are in greater demand than those involving manual labour.
options.C: The government’s jobs guarantee programme makes low-level management jobs available across all industries to all graduates in the nation.
options.D: A bus driver becomes an app creator and, in the course of one month, reaches one million downloads on Playstore with a four-star rating.

infoBite: Annihilation of Caste (1936) was written as a speech for the Jat-Pat-Todak Mandal of Lahore, which cancelled it; Ambedkar printed it himself. A shows birth fixing occupation; B shows labour graded high and low.

question:
Imagine that you’re in a game show and your host shows you three doors. Behind one of them is a shiny car and behind the others are goats. You pick one of the doors and get what lies within. After making your choice, your host chooses to open one of the other two doors, which inevitably reveals a goat. He then asks you if you want to stick with your original pick, or switch to the other remaining door. What do you do? Most people think that it doesn’t make a difference and they tend to stick with their first pick. With two doors left, you should have a 50% chance of selecting the one with the car. If you agree, then you have just fallen afoul of one of the most infamous mathematical problems – the Monty Hall Problem. In reality, you should switch every time which doubles your odds of getting the car. Over the years, the problem has ensnared countless people, but not, it seems, pigeons. The humble pigeon can learn with practice the best tactic for the Monty Hall Problem, switching from their initial choice almost every time. Amazingly, humans do not!
(Adapted from an article by Ed Yong in Discover Magazine.)
Which of the following conclusions follow from the passage above?

options.A: Humans calculate the probability of independent, random events such as the opening of a door by dividing the specific outcomes by the total number of possible outcomes.
options.B: Humans find it very difficult to learn to account for the host’s hand in making the event non-random and, thereby, changing the outcome of the event.
options.C: Calculating probabilities is difficult for humans but easy for pigeons; which is why the pigeons succeed where the humans fail.
options.D: Humans are governed by reason, but pigeons are irrational and only interested in the outcome and will do whatever it takes to get food.

infoBite: Switching wins two times out of three, because the host always opens a goat door — his choice isn't random. People treat it as a fresh 50–50, which is option A's error.

question:
The truth is that, despite the recent success of car-makers P and Q, India’s automobile industry is in a state not that different from the bad old days of the license-permit quota raj when two carmakers dominated a captive domestic market with substandard vehicles and with very little, if any, research and development, and low to negligible productivity growth. High tariff barriers have certainly induced foreign automobile makers to enter the Indian market by setting up local operations, but this so-called “tariff jumping” foreign investment has produced an industry that is inefficient, operating generally at a low scale, and whose products are not globally competitive either in terms of cost or of innovation. It is noteworthy that the automobile parts industry, which has faced low tariffs (as low as 12.5%) and has been largely deregulated, has been characterised by higher productivity and much better export performance than the completely-built units’ sector in the years since liberalisation.
(Adapted from an Op-Ed in The Mint.)
Which of the following statements can be inferred from the above?

options.B: Tariff jumping leads to increases in productivity.
options.C: Deregulation has worked for the automotive parts industry and therefore should be applied to completely-built units.
options.D: P and Q do not invest enough in research and development.

infoBite: The parts sector (low tariffs, deregulated) outperforms the protected car sector, and the industry is said to do little R&D. Tariff jumping is blamed for inefficiency, so B is wrong.

question: Which of the following texts is a collection of stories that a group of pilgrims tell each other?
infoBite: Chaucer's pilgrims meet at the Tabard Inn, Southwark, and the host Harry Bailly proposes a tale-telling contest on the way to Becket's shrine. Parliament of Fowls is Chaucer's dream vision; Spenser's Calender is 1579, Bunyan's allegory 1678.

question: Which of these is NOT an autobiography?

options.A: Baby Kamble, The Prisons We Broke

infoBite: Untouchable (1935) is Anand's novel about Bakha, with a preface by E. M. Forster. Karukku (1992, Tamil), Jina Amucha (Marathi) and Joothan (1997, Hindi) are Dalit autobiographies — the last two were asked again in GATE 2024.

question: Writers Workshop and Blaft are ________________.

options.A: niche publishing houses in India that focus on particular genres
options.B: little magazines that were set up by small collectives of writers

infoBite: P. Lal founded Writers Workshop in Calcutta in 1958; it printed early books by many Indian English poets. Blaft, a Chennai press, is known for translated Tamil pulp fiction.

question:
The following lines capture the central trope of a well-known 18th century satirical tract.
“I have been assured by a very knowing American of my acquaintance in London, that a young healthy child, well nursed, is, at a year old, a most delicious, nourishing, and wholesome food...”
Identify the tract from the options below.
infoBite: Swift's A Modest Proposal (1729) ironically suggests the Irish poor sell their children as food. Bacon's essay is “Of Death” (quoted in GATE 2022); Mill's On Liberty is 1859.

question: Whose poem does Cleanth Brooks close-read to arrive at his concept of “the well-wrought urn”?
infoBite: The Well Wrought Urn (1947) includes “Keats's Sylvan Historian”, a reading of “Ode on a Grecian Urn”. The title phrase itself comes from Donne's “The Canonization”. Brooks's “paradox” was asked in GATE 2023.

question: What is common among Charles Dickens’ A Tale of Two Cities, Mahasweta Devi’s Mother of 1084, Shobha Shakti’s Gorilla, and Chimamanda Ngozi Adichie’s Half of A Yellow Sun?

options.A: These novels are set during times of political uprisings.
options.C: These novels have animals as central characters.

infoBite: French Revolution (Dickens, 1859); Naxalite movement (Mahasweta Devi's Hajar Churashir Maa, 1974); Sri Lankan civil war (Shobasakthi); Biafran war (Adichie, 2006). A Tale of Two Cities also came up in GATE 2022 and 2026.

question: Henry James’ essay “The Art of Fiction”, one of the earliest literary critical engagements with the form of the novel, was preceded by his book-length study of _______________.
infoBite: James's Hawthorne (1879) appeared in the English Men of Letters series; “The Art of Fiction” (1884) answered Walter Besant's lecture on the novel. Faulkner was born only in 1897.

question: Which of the following is NOT true of Bram Stoker’s Dracula?

options.A: It is considered to be a gothic novel.
options.B: It is narrated mostly through letters.
options.C: Transylvania is an important setting in the novel.

infoBite: Dracula (1897) is an epistolary Gothic novel told through letters, diaries and news cuttings, opening with Jonathan Harker's journey to Transylvania. A bildungsroman follows a hero's growing up, as in Great Expectations.

question:
“The name is H. Hatterr, and I am continuing . . .
Biologically, I am fifty-five of the species.”
The lines above are from an early Indian English novel. Who is the author of this novel?
infoBite: All About H. Hatterr (1948) is narrated by an Anglo-Malay hero in comic, mangled English; Rushdie called it an influence. It was asked again in GATE 2025 (works not by Anita Desai).

question: In Areopagitica, John Milton made an impassioned appeal _______________.

options.A: against censorship and for freedom of expression
options.B: for legal reform allowing divorce based on spousal incompatibility
options.C: for freedom of the church from royal control
options.D: against slavery in the New World

works: The Doctrine and Discipline of Divorce
infoBite: Areopagitica (1644) attacks Parliament's Licensing Order of 1643; its title recalls the Areopagus of Athens. Option B describes Milton's divorce tracts, such as The Doctrine and Discipline of Divorce (1643).

question: Which one of the following texts propounds the aesthetic theory of ‘rasa’?
infoBite: Bharata's Nāṭyaśāstra says rasa arises from vibhāva, anubhāva and vyabhicāribhāva. Rasa came up again in GATE 2024 and 2025; Śākuntalam is Kālidāsa's play, the Charaka Samhita a medical text.

question: Which of the following novels is/are predominantly set in Bombay?
infoBite: Ravan and Eddie is set in a Bombay chawl; A Fine Balance in an unnamed “city by the sea”; Saleem grows up at Methwold's Estate in Bombay. The White Tiger (Booker 2008) moves from Laxmangarh to Delhi and Bangalore.

question: Which of the following critically rewrite/s canonical English novels?
infoBite: Foe (1986) retells Robinson Crusoe through Susan Barton; Wide Sargasso Sea (1966) gives Jane Eyre's Bertha a past as Antoinette. Ice-Candy-Man is a Partition novel; The Famished Road won the 1991 Booker.

question: Of the following, which novelist/s combine/s feminist concerns with magic realism?
infoBite: In Morrison's Beloved (1987) the ghost of Sethe's dead daughter returns in bodily form. Alexievich (Nobel 2015) writes documentary oral history. Magic realism was asked in GATE 2022, 2023 and 2024 too.

question: In which of these Shakespearean plays do important female characters disguise themselves as men?
infoBite: Portia becomes the lawyer Balthazar, Rosalind becomes Ganymede and Viola becomes Cesario. A Midsummer Night's Dream has fairies and a love potion but no cross-dressing.

question: The following words in English are clustered according to their origin. Choose the cluster/s that contain/s words drawn from languages of the Indian subcontinent.
infoBite: Kedgeree (khichri), shampoo (champo), Juggernaut (Jagannath), calico (Calicut) and bungalow (bangla) come from the subcontinent; Hobson-Jobson (1886) lists such words. Cluster C comes from Greek myth and the Bible.

question: Which of the following is/are true of Charlotte Brontë’s Jane Eyre?

options.A: It was published under the pen-name Currer Bell.
options.B: It was published originally in three volumes.
options.C: It has been read as a critique of heterosexual romance, marriage, and domesticity.
options.D: The story is told from the point of view of a “madwoman in the attic”.

infoBite: Jane Eyre (1847) came out in three volumes, “edited by Currer Bell”. Jane narrates it herself; the madwoman is Bertha Mason (Gilbert and Gubar's 1979 title, asked GATE 2024). Also asked in GATE 2022 and 2026.

question: Which of the following is an example/are examples of noir, popular both as fiction and film?
infoBite: Chandler's The Big Sleep (1939, Philip Marlowe) and Hammett's The Maltese Falcon (1930, Sam Spade) became noir films in 1946 and 1941. Christie's novel is a classic whodunit; Fargo (1996) is a Coen brothers film, not a novel.

question: Which of the following use/s the device of a ‘story within a story’ with multiple narrators?

options.A: A Portrait of an Artist as a Young Man

works: A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man
infoBite: Lockwood records Nelly Dean's story in Wuthering Heights (1847); an unnamed narrator on the Thames passes on Marlow's tale in Heart of Darkness (1899). Heart of Darkness was also asked in GATE 2024 and 2025.
note: The paper prints “A Portrait of an Artist”; Joyce's title is A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man.

question:
Match the following plays with genre or style:
i. Hayavadana
ii. Harvest
iii. Ghashiram Kotwal
iv. Evam Indrajit

a. Political satire
b. Modernist play reworking the folk
c. Theatre of the absurd
d. Futuristic dystopia
infoBite: Hayavadana (1971) reworks a folk tale in Yakshagana style; Harvest (1997) is set in a future organ trade; Ghashiram Kotwal (1972) satirises Peshwa-era power; Badal Sircar's Evam Indrajit (1963) is absurdist. Hayavadana and Harvest recur in GATE 2023 and 2024.

question:
Study the three examples below:
i) In George Orwell’s novel 1984, the interior ministry of the totalitarian state is called the ‘Ministry of Love’.
ii) In the genre of horror fiction, the reader knows that the killer is hiding in the closet, but the protagonist does not.
iii) “But Brutus says he was ambitious; And Brutus is an honourable man.” (William Shakespeare, Julius Caesar)
These are instances of _______________.
infoBite: Three kinds of irony: an ironic name (the Ministry of Love tortures), dramatic irony (the reader knows more than the hero) and verbal irony in Mark Antony's speech. The same speech was asked for paralipsis in GATE 2025.

question: An “implied reader” is a _______________.

options.A: reader who participates in creating the meaning of a text
options.C: hypothetical reader, not the actual reader, that the text addresses
options.D: reader who reads critically against the grain of the text

infoBite: Wolfgang Iser's The Implied Reader (1972) names the reader a text is built for, as against any actual reader. It pairs with Wayne Booth's “implied author” in The Rhetoric of Fiction (1961).

question:
Read the following:
“[…] a text is made of multiple writings, drawn from many cultures and entering into mutual relations of dialogue, parody, contestation, but there is one place where this multiplicity is focused and that place is the reader, not, as was hitherto said, the author. […] the birth of the reader must be at the cost of the death of the Author.”
Which theoretical school does the excerpt best represent?
infoBite: This is the ending of Barthes's “The Death of the Author” (1967), a key post-structuralist essay. It was asked again in GATE 2022, so learn its closing line.

question: Literary criticism considers which one of the following texts as offering the strongest support for mimetic theories of art?
infoBite: Aristotle defines tragedy as an imitation (mimesis) of an action and defends it; Plato also calls art imitation but attacks it. Abrams's The Mirror and the Lamp (1953) sorts theories as mimetic, pragmatic, expressive and objective.

question:
The following is a passage about O. V. Vijayan’s The Legends of Khasak:
The novel is set in a remote village, in the middle of the 20th century. The narrative is replete with images of the vast ecosystem of the living and the non-living, a land potent with dreams and legends.
The analysis presented in this description is congruent with which one of the following concepts proposed by Mikhail Bakhtin?
works: Forms of Time and of the Chronotope in the Novel
infoBite: Chronotope (“time-space”) is how a narrative fuses a place and a period. The Legends of Khasak (Khasakkinte Itihasam, 1969) is a Malayalam classic. Bakhtin's carnivalesque was asked in GATE 2022.

question: Which one of the following did NOT happen in 1919, the year the First World War ended?

options.A: The Progressive Writers’ Association was formed in India.
options.B: The radical political activist and philosopher Rosa Luxemborg was murdered.
options.D: James Joyce’s Ulysses was being serialised.

infoBite: The Progressive Writers' Association held its first conference in Lucknow in 1936 under Premchand (asked GATE 2024). Tagore gave up his knighthood after the Jallianwala Bagh massacre; Ulysses ran in The Little Review from 1918.
note: The paper spells the name “Luxemborg”; the usual spelling is Luxemburg.

question:
Assertion P: Dalit narratives tend to be read single-dimensionally as evoking the reader’s pity at the protagonist’s caste humiliation, or as telling the story of heroic protest against discrimination, or as a description of the protagonist’s rise from misery to triumph.
Assertion Q: There is a tendency to keep the Other in the space of difference, as perpetually exotic.
In the context of the assertions above, which one of the following statements is true?

options.A: P and Q are contradictory assertions.
options.B: P and Q are compatible assertions.
options.C: P and Q cannot be read in relation to each other.
options.D: Q is the only explanation for P.

infoBite: Both describe a reductive reading: Dalit texts are boxed into fixed scripts (P), just as the Other is kept exotic (Q). They fit together, but nothing says Q is the only cause of P.

question:
Some of the recent novels of the Brazilian writer Paulo Coelho were published in multiple languages simultaneously, or immediately after the Portuguese edition.
Which of the following is this phenomenon NOT an evidence of?

options.A: Rebecca Walkowitz’s argument that novels are often ‘born translated’
options.B: The globality of marketplace for books
options.D: The ‘nation’ as the sole frame for understanding literature

infoBite: Walkowitz's Born Translated (2015) studies novels written for global translation from the start. Simultaneous editions undercut the nation as the only frame; Coelho is best known for The Alchemist.

question:
Match the authors in the first column with their respective translators in the second column.
i. Madhavikutty
ii. U. R. Ananthamurthy
iii. Indira Goswami
iv. Namdeo Dhasal

a. A. K. Ramanujan
b. Dilip Chitre
c. Kamala Das
d. Aruni Kashyap
infoBite: Madhavikutty is Kamala Das's Malayalam pen-name, so she translated herself. Ramanujan translated Ananthamurthy's Samskara (1976); Dilip Chitre translated the Dalit Panther poet Namdeo Dhasal; Aruni Kashyap translates Goswami from Assamese.

question: Which of the following is/are true about Gilles Deleuze and Felix Guattari’s conception of ‘minor literature’?

options.A: The discussion focuses on the writing of Franz Kafka.
options.B: Minor literature is literature that a minority produces in a major language.
options.C: Minor literature is a form of popular literature.
options.D: Minor literature is literature in a minor language.

infoBite: In Kafka: Toward a Minor Literature (1975), Kafka, a Prague Jew writing in German, is the model. Minor literature is deterritorialised, political and collective — written by a minority inside a major language.

question:
Quote P:
“O wild West Wind, thou breath of Autumn's being,
Thou, from whose unseen presence the leaves dead
Are driven, like ghosts from an enchanter fleeing,
Yellow, and black, and pale, and hectic red,
Pestilence-stricken multitudes: O thou,
Who chariotest to their dark wintry bed
[…]”
Quote Q:
“O golden-tongued Romance with serene lute!
Fair plumed Siren! Queen of far away!”
Which of the following is/are correct?

options.A: Both quotes are examples of apostrophe.
options.C: Both quotes are examples of aporia.
options.D: Both quotes are examples of personification.

works: On Sitting Down to Read King Lear Once Again
infoBite: Both address and personify an abstraction: Shelley's “Ode to the West Wind” (1819, terza rima) and Keats's sonnet “On Sitting Down to Read King Lear Once Again” (1818). Apostrophe was asked again in GATE 2024.

question:
Prolepsis is the representation or assumption in the present, of a future act or development.
Which of the following is/are instance/s of prolepsis?

options.A: “Six decades later she would describe how at the age of thirteen she had written her way through a whole history of literature.” Ian McEwan, Atonement.
options.B: “Horatio, I am dead.” William Shakespeare, Hamlet.
options.C: “In my younger and more vulnerable years my father gave me some advice that I’ve been turning over in my head ever since.” F. Scott Fitzgerald, The Great Gatsby.
options.D: “Many years later, as he faced the firing squad, Colonel Aureliano Buendía was to remember that distant afternoon when his father took him to discover ice.” Gabriel García Márquez, One Hundred Years of Solitude.

infoBite: Prolepsis is a flash-forward; Hamlet speaks of his death before it happens (Act 5, Scene 2). Nick Carraway's opening looks back, not forward. The Márquez line is the famous first sentence of the 1967 novel.

question: Gayatri Chakravorty Spivak’s essay “Can the Subaltern Speak?” proposes which of the following?

options.A: The voice of the subaltern is appropriated by ‘intellectuals’ desiring to speak for the subaltern.
options.B: It is easy to confuse writing about the subaltern with the subaltern speaking for herself.
options.C: All women are subaltern and therefore cannot truly speak.
options.D: The ‘intellectuals’ speaking for the subaltern and the subaltern speaking for herself can be equivalent.

infoBite: Spivak's essay (1988) faults Foucault and Deleuze for speaking for the oppressed, and reads sati and the suicide of Bhubaneswari Bhaduri. Spivak was also asked in GATE 2023 (Derrida translation).

question: Which of the following is/are example/s of ‘metafiction’?

options.A: Each chapter in a novel is narrated by a different character.
options.B: The reader is a character in the novel who interrupts the story because he realises that he is reading an incomplete text.
options.C: The narrator of the novel travels into the wild and encounters a man who embodies the horrors of colonial power. The latter then proceeds to tell his story.
options.D: A character in a novel encounters a shabbily dressed man. Soon, this man lets us, the readers, know that he is the author of the novel and is contemplating the future of this character.

works: If on a Winter's Night a Traveller
infoBite: Metafiction draws attention to itself as fiction. B describes Calvino's If on a Winter's Night a Traveller (asked GATE 2023); D recalls the author's appearance in Fowles's The French Lieutenant's Woman. C is simply a frame story.

question:
Choose one or more options from below.
In contrast to traditional Historicism, New Historicism ________________.

options.A: rejects the idea that history is an objective narrative of events unfolding in linear time
options.B: does not make strict distinctions between literary and non-literary texts
options.C: takes a particular interest in the textualisation of the material world
options.D: takes history only to be a background and context for understanding literary texts

infoBite: Stephen Greenblatt named New Historicism in 1982; Louis Montrose summed it up as “the historicity of texts and the textuality of history”. Treating history as mere background (D) is the old historicism.

question:
“The feminist insistence that ‘the personal is political’ has had profound effects on other genres. Feminist academics in several disciplines now insist that the subjective element must not be left out of the practice of research methods, such as the interview, or of theories of knowledge production (Skeggs 1995; Maynard and Purvis 1994; Reinharz 1992).”
From the passage above, which of the following can be correctly concluded?

options.A: The passage argues that interviews and theories of knowledge production are not examples of research methods.
options.B: ‘The personal is political’ is a feminist argument.
options.C: Skeggs, Maynard, Purvis, and Reinharz are names of feminist scholars.
options.D: The passage argues that the subjective can legitimately be part of research methods.

infoBite: “The personal is political” became a second-wave slogan and is linked to Carol Hanisch's 1970 essay of that title. The passage calls the interview a research method, so A is wrong.

question:
“ARE YOU DARK? OR VERY LIGHT?” Revelation came.
“You mean—like plain or milk chocolate?”
Her assent was clinical, crushing in its light
Impersonality. Rapidly, wave-length adjusted,
I chose. “West African sepia”—and as afterthought,
“Down in my passport.” Silence for spectroscopic
Flight of fancy, till truthfulness clanged her accent
Hard on the mouthpiece. “WHAT’S THAT?” conceding
“DON’T KNOW WHAT THAT IS.” “Like brunette.”
“THAT’S DARK, ISN’T IT?” “Not altogether.
Facially, I am brunette, but, madam, you should see
The rest of me. Palm of my hand, soles of my feet
Are a peroxide blond. Friction, caused—
Foolishly, madam—by sitting down, has turned
My bottom raven black—One moment, madam!”—sensing
Her receiver rearing on the thunderclap
About my ears—“Madam,” I pleaded, “wouldn’t you rather
See for yourself?”
In Wole Soyinka’s “Telephone Conversation”, the man seeking to rent a room responds to the white landlady’s racism by _________________.

options.A: describing black as a spectrum as opposed to a single colour
options.B: being the subservient Black man, who concedes to her definition of race
options.C: locating race squarely in her ways of seeing

infoBite: Soyinka's poem satirises a London landlady's racism through a phone call about a room. Soyinka won the Nobel Prize in 1986, the first African laureate.

question: In Arthur Conan Doyle’s writings featuring Sherlock Holmes, as is the case with much of 19th century British fiction, colonialism appears as objects, events, animals, places, fears and desires. Which of the following support/s this claim?

options.A: Opium dens in London, frequented by Holmes
options.B: The war in which Watson served as a doctor
options.C: The hound in The Hound of the Baskervilles
options.D: The pet animals in “The Adventure of the Speckled Band”

works: The Man with the Twisted Lip
The Adventure of the Speckled Band
infoBite: Watson was wounded in the Afghan war (A Study in Scarlet, 1887); Holmes visits an opium den in “The Man with the Twisted Lip”; Dr Roylott brings a swamp adder, cheetah and baboon back from India. The hound is an English legend.

question:
“My Papa’s Waltz” by Theodore Roethke
The whiskey on your breath
Could make a small boy dizzy;
But I hung on like death:
Such waltzing was not easy.

We romped until the pans
Slid from the kitchen shelf;
My mother’s countenance
Could not unfrown itself.

The hand that held my wrist
Was battered on one knuckle;
At every step you missed
My right ear scraped a buckle.

You beat time on my head
With a palm caked hard by dirt,
Then waltzed me off to bed
Still clinging to your shirt.
Which of the following can be observed about this poem?

options.A: The form of the poem is that of the Petrarchan sonnet.
options.B: There is a simile in the first stanza.
options.C: Images in the last two stanzas suggest that the father is a working-class man.
options.D: The poem is in rhyming couplets.

infoBite: Four quatrains rhyming ABAB in trimeter (1942), so neither a sonnet nor couplets. “Hung on like death” is the simile; the battered knuckle and dirt-caked palm mark a labourer.

question: What does MLA stand for in literary studies?
infoBite: The Modern Language Association (founded 1883) publishes the MLA Handbook, the citation style used most in literary studies. APA and Chicago are the other common styles.
note: NTA's final answer key for this paper isn't publicly readable, so this answer was checked by Claude, not copied from the key.

question: Which of the following is not a poem by Emily Dickinson?

options.A: Because I could not stop for Death
options.B: Remember me when I am gone away
options.D: I like a look of Agony

works: Because I could not stop for Death
I like a look of Agony
infoBite: “Remember” (“Remember me when I am gone away”) is a sonnet by Christina Rossetti (1862). “I like a look of Agony” was also asked in GATE 2024.
note: NTA's final answer key for this paper isn't publicly readable, so this answer was checked by Claude, not copied from the key.

question:
Arrange the following works in the chronological order of their publication:
A. A Woman Killed with Kindness
B. The Shoemaker's Holiday

question:
[Poem: Queen Elizabeth I, 'When I was fair and young']
When I was fair and young, and favour graced me,
Of many was I sought, their mistress for to be;
But I did scorn them all, and answered them therefore,
'Go, go, go, seek some otherwhere,
Importune me no more!'

How many weeping eyes I made to pine with woe,
How many sighing hearts, I have no skill to show;
Yet I the prouder grew, and answered them therefore,
'Go, go, go, seek some otherwhere,
Importune me no more!'

"Go, go, go, seek some otherwhere,
Importune me no more!"'

question:
[Passage: Angelo's soliloquy, Shakespeare, Measure for Measure, Act 2, Scene 2]
What's this, what's this? Is this her fault or mine?
The tempter or the tempted, who sins most? Ha!
Not she; nor doth she tempt: but it is I
That, lying by the violet in the sun,
Do as the carrion does, not as the flower,
Corrupt with virtuous season. …
Thieves for their robbery have authority
When judges steal themselves. What, do I love her,
That I desire to hear her speak again,
And feast upon her eyes? What is't I dream on?
O cunning enemy, that, to catch a saint,
With saints dost bait thy hook! Most dangerous
Is that temptation that doth goad us on
To sin in loving virtue: never could the strumpet,
With all her double vigour, art and nature,
Once stir my temper; but this virtuous maid
Subdues me quite. Even till now,
When men were fond, I smiled and wonder'd how.

'Thieves for their robbery have authority / When judges steal themselves' implies that:
infoBite: Angelo, the strict deputy judging Claudio, sees that his own desire for Isabella would make him a worse thief than those he condemns.

question:
[Passage: John Ruskin, Modern Painters, vol. 1, 'Definition of Greatness in Art', summarised with key lines] Painting, with all its technicalities, is 'nothing but a noble and expressive language, invaluable as the vehicle of thought, but by itself nothing'. One who can represent natural objects faithfully has 'only learned the language by which his thoughts are to be expressed'. Painting, like speech, has its grammar and melody; it 'possesses more power of delighting the sense, while it speaks to the intellect'. 'It is not by the mode of representing and saying, but by what is represented and said, that the respective greatness either of the painter or the writer is to be finally determined.'

What implicit assumption about language and expression underpins the passage's argument?

options.A: All forms of art must use written language to be effective.
options.B: Expression without technical skill is more valuable.
options.C: The medium of expression is secondary to the message conveyed.
options.D: The value of grammar and melody lies in their aesthetic, not communicative, power.

infoBite: Ruskin treats painting as a language whose worth lies in the thought it carries. Modern Painters (1843–60) began as a defence of J. M. W. Turner.
